He claims to have a piece of the Roswell crash," which, if true, would put physical debris from that event in a private collection abroad.
japanese-musha-experiment-in-transmissio: A Japanese researcher named Takaaki Musha ran an experiment, described in a paper, in which the whole device was submerged in transmission oil and, Michels says, the team reported a successful result. Michels recalls this himself from the paper without giving details of the device, as an example of fringe propulsion work that claims to have worked.
jared-birchall-a-mormon-elder-as-elon-mu: A Mormon elder named Jared Birchall is, in effect, the handler of the businessman Elon Musk: "the man who manages all of his affairs." The researcher Matthew Pines says this in a 2024 talk with Michels and names no source. He offers it as a connection worth noticing, because if true it would put a church figure at the center of one of the best-known businessmen's lives.
jason-sands-radars-at-roswell-and-white-: The story is that powerful radar stations in New Mexico, at Roswell and at White Sands, knocked UFOs out of the sky in 1947. Michels passes it on from a man named Jason Sands, who talked about it with Joe Rogan: high-powered radar "disrupting the flight paths of the crafts." A former scientist at DARPA, the Pentagon's advanced research agency, named John Blitch, sketches how it might have gone. The radar was moved out to the desert, White Sands being "a natural place to do that," the power was turned up, and "the next thing you know" a flying saucer came down, during a storm. An online researcher who goes by UAPGerb says it outright: alien spaceships crashed because of high-powered radar, the government now had their bodies, and Presidents Harry Truman and Dwight D. Eisenhower had to decide what to do about it. In another episode Michels credits the idea to Philip J. Corso's 1997 book The Day After Roswell and others, and calls it a kind of "directed energy attack," naming the researcher Steven Greer as well. None of the tellers says they saw it. They pass on what they have heard or read, and if it were true it would mean the US accidentally learned how to bring down alien craft.
jason-sands-they-want-their-stuff-back: Whoever owns the material held in a secret program wants it returned, and they are "going to kill everybody involved in the program if they don't get it", according to a man named Jason Sands. Michels repeats this second-hand, saying Sands said it on the show of the interviewer Joe Rogan. Taken at face value, it would mean the program is holding something its owners want back and are willing to fight for.
javanese-cemetery-marriage-and-sex-ritua: Peter Levenda, whom the episode bills as a CIA historian, says there are cemeteries in Java, Indonesia, where people perform a ritual of marriage and sex at a grave, and that he visited one in particular, at the grave of a prince. He tells Michels it is true and that he saw the place himself.
jay-stratton-s-three-star-slide-shown-to: A government official named Jay Stratton showed members of Congress a slide of what was presented as a UFO but was really just three stars, according to the UFO skeptic Mick West. West tells it without naming a source, placing it somewhere between 2019 and 2021. He offers it as an example of ordinary things being passed off to lawmakers as unexplained.
jc-said-navy-running-majestic-12-was-rig: Around 1996 in Los Angeles, the television writer Bryce Zabel says a source he calls JC told him that his show had got some things right, including making the head of Majestic 12, a rumoured secret group said to manage the UFO question, a Navy man. Zabel tells it from his own meeting with JC. If true, it would mean the real group, or something like it, was run out of the Navy.
jean-louis-naudin-s-vacuum-tube-tests: A French experimenter named Jean-Louis Naudin is said to have run his tests inside vacuum tubes, so that air could not be the cause of what he saw. The British computer hacker Gary McKinnon mentions this in passing to Michels, saying simply, "He's done it in vacuum tubes," without describing the tests further. McKinnon raises it because a result that holds in a vacuum would point to something more than ordinary air effects.
jeffrey-epstein-tape-with-steve-bannon-a: In a taped interview with the political strategist Steve Bannon, the financier Jeffrey Epstein gets many things wrong yet still sounds like a man who had been talking to people who knew what they were talking about, according to the mathematician Eric Weinstein, who has listened to it. Weinstein points to the errors: Epstein claims he founded the Santa Fe Institute, a research centre, around 1990 to 1993, when others founded it in 1984, and he garbles a point about quarks and the physicist Murray Gell-Mann. To Weinstein, the tape is a muddled echo of real insiders' knowledge.
jeffrey-kripal-s-compilation-of-anomalie: A researcher named Jeffrey Kripal is said to have gathered hundreds and hundreds of anomalies, strange events that don't fit ordinary explanations, into one collection. The skeptic Michael Shermer mentions this work in passing while debating Michels, naming it as an example of this kind of research without going into any one case.
jeffrey-kripal-s-mit-lecture-on-flying-s: The religion scholar Jeffrey Kripal once gave a lecture at MIT, the Massachusetts university, on saints who were said to fly, and in the audience was the head of revolutionary technologies at Skunk Works, the secret aircraft-design unit of the company Lockheed Martin. Michels tells this himself, without naming the Lockheed man or his source. The point is that a top weapons engineer would take an interest in stories of levitating saints.
jeffrey-kripal-s-night-experience-sharin: The scholar Jeffrey Kripal is said to have shared a room with Whitley Strieber, a writer he wrote a book with, at the Esalen Institute, a retreat center in California. In the middle of the night Kripal had an experience, and all he could think was, "oh my god, this is real and it's happening now." Jeffrey Mishlove, an interviewer with a PhD who studies the paranormal, retells it as Kripal tells it.
jellyfish-probe-the-radar-beam-and-are-s: Objects nicknamed "Jellyfish" for their shape have been picked up on radar about 6 kilometres north and south of a site run by Skywatcher, a startup that tries to call in UFOs and track them. The company's team says they saw these objects probing their radar beam, and that in February 2025 they saw for the first time "how two Jellyfish fly together on the radar." They tell it as their own observation, which would mean the objects react to being watched and sometimes travel in pairs.
jellyfish-uap-debunked: An unidentified object that became known as the "jellyfish" UAP (UAP is the US government's term for unidentified flying or anomalous objects) turned out to be nothing unexplained, according to an unnamed speaker in a clip played on the show. The speaker says "it ended up being debunked" and "was not a UAP."
jellyfish-uap-explained-as-a-group-of-dr: The jellyfish, an unexplained flying object on video that is said to look like a jellyfish, may really be a group of drones linked to each other "Bluetooth or whatever" and flying together in coordination. The researcher and skeptic Michael Shermer suggests this in a 2026 debate with Michels and names no source. If he is right, the object is ordinary technology and nothing unknown.
jeremy-corbell-and-the-missing-page-of-t: A government document about unexplained aerial sightings, released in 2024 by the journalist Michael Shellenberger, was said to be missing a page, and the UFO filmmaker Jeremy Corbell spoke out about it at length, including that a name had been taken off it. The musician Flying Lotus, a hip hop artist who follows the subject, recalls this, naming the journalist George Knapp and Matthew Brown alongside Corbell. He says the whole affair rubbed him the wrong way, as if something had been cut from the public record.
jesse-feels-strieber-s-implant-2020: Michels says he touched an implant in the body of the writer Whitley Strieber, who says he has met aliens, and calls it "the weirdest thing in the world." Michels tells it as his own experience and adds that Strieber says the object moves with his own metabolism, as if it were alive in him. In a later episode Michels tells it more briefly and places it in Strieber's ear: "I felt an implant in his ear."
jesse-marcel-library-posts-article-about: In 2025, Greg Rogers, a doctor billed as a NASA doctor, says he recently found out that the Jesse Marcel Library in Montana, named for a man named Jesse Marcel Sr., "has put up an article about me in their library". Rogers tells it himself, as a sign that his story has been taken up by people who keep records on UFOs.
jesse-marcel-s-unbendable-foil-thin-meta: In 1947, at the Roswell crash site in New Mexico, debris was found that was thin as foil yet strange, according to Jesse Marcel Sr., the Army Air Force intelligence officer who says he picked it up. In a recording played on the podcast, he describes "a piece of metal" about two feet wide and two or three feet long that "felt like you had nothing in your hands" and "wasn't any thicker than the foil out of a pack of cigarettes." Michels gives the second telling, from an interview by the journalist Bob Pratt. He credits it to Jesse Marcel Jr. and calls him the intelligence officer at the site, which differs from the first telling. In Michels's version, the foil-like debris did not burn when someone held a lighter to it. If the accounts are right, the wreckage was made of no material anyone knew.
jesse-marcel-says-weather-balloon-was-a-: In 1978, Lieutenant Colonel Jesse Marcel, an officer who handled the 1947 crash debris at Roswell, New Mexico, is said to have come forward and called the official weather balloon explanation "just a cover story." Michels tells this himself several times. He adds that Marcel said he was forced to pose for a photo with balloon material. In another telling Michels dates it to 1979 and says Marcel claimed to have handled "memory metal," a metal that springs back to its shape. Bob Lazar, a well-known figure in UFO circles, passes on Marcel's point that the material in the press photos taken under General Roger Ramey "wasn't the stuff that we found." If true, it would mean the military swapped out the real wreckage to hide what it had recovered.
jesse-michels-also-told-of-an-incoming-c: Jesse Michels says that he too was told a craft was coming toward Earth. He says so himself in 2026, in a conversation with the filmmaker Jeremy Corbell, when the talk turned to claims passed around by intelligence sources about an object slowly heading our way.
jesse-s-contact-with-astrid-stuckelberge: In 2023 a woman named Astrid Stuckelberger, who had something to tell, emailed Jesse Michels to say, in his words, "We must talk now", and then she went silent. Michels tells this himself on an episode about Jeffrey Epstein and claims of a hidden global cabal. He tells it as an odd moment where a would-be witness reached out urgently and then disappeared.
jesse-s-conversation-with-tulsi-gabbard-: Michels says that in 2025 he had a short talk about UAP, the US government's term for UFOs, with Tulsi Gabbard, the US Director of National Intelligence, who oversees the country's spy agencies. He says this himself, as something he took part in, during an episode with a former Senate staffer named Kirk McConnell. He gives no details of what was said, only that he raised the topic with her, which would matter because she is one of the most senior intelligence officials in the country.
jesse-s-france-trip-and-the-before-sunse: Jesse Michels says that one day, on a whim, he booked a trip to France, stayed the whole summer, and ended up dating a girl in Paris. He links this to Before Sunset, a film by the director Richard Linklater about a romance in Paris. Michels tells it from his own life, in a talk about synchronicities and prophetic dreams, as an example of life matching a story in a way that feels meant.
jesse-s-interview-with-puthoff-and-weins: Michels says a subject came up in his earlier conversation with the researchers Hal Puthoff and Eric Weinstein: remote viewing, the claimed ability to describe faraway places or things using only the mind. He mentions it himself, as something he took part in, while talking with a Navy scientist named Salvatore Pais, who is known for UFO-related patents, and he notes that Puthoff had touched on the topic in that interview.
jesse-s-month-of-bad-luck-after-the-visi: Michels says that after a visit tied to the story of a strange ranch, he had a month of bad luck in Los Angeles, including the day an armed gunman ran into the building where he works. He tells this himself, as something that happened to him. The suggestion is that the visit may have brought trouble home with it.
jesse-visits-aztec-crash-site-with-the-r: Michels says he went to the place near Aztec, New Mexico, where a craft is said to have crashed in 1948, together with Scott and Suzanne Ramsey, researchers who he says have put "$600,000 plus" into the case over decades and have "so much evidence." He says the visit was filmed and that you can still see trees splintered where a craft seemed to have been dragged out. In one telling he only says he went with his editor. In another he brings up FBI files on Silas Newton, a man tied to early stories about the crash. Michels tells it from his own visit, as physical traces that a real crash took place.
jesse-visits-the-richter-island-site-at-: There is a small island just off the coast near Bariloche, a town in Argentina, tied to a scientist named Ronald Richter, and Jesse Michels says he has been there and seen it himself. He mentions it in passing, "a little island off the coast", while talking with the researcher Jason Jorjani about claims of a secret Nazi flying-saucer effort. For Michels it is a real place he can vouch for in a story that otherwise lives in old records.
jessica-utts-presidential-address-on-psy: A statistician named Jessica Utts, who had studied the evidence for psychic abilities, went on to become president of the American Statistical Association, the main professional body for statisticians in the United States, and in 2016 gave a presidential address on that evidence. The writer Eric Wargo, who studies precognitive dreams, mentions this to Michels, recalling that she "was the president of the American statistical society" one year. He tells it to show that the data on psychic functioning was taken seriously by someone at the top of her field.
jessica-utts-review-of-stargate-document: A statistician named Jessica Utts is said to have reviewed the data from Stargate, a US government programme that studied remote viewing, the claimed ability to describe faraway places with the mind, and to have concluded there was something real in it. Michels tells this many times, sometimes on his own and sometimes from what guests have told him. He says Utts was president of the American Statistical Association, that she did the review for the CIA around 1995 alongside the psychologist Ray Hyman, a total skeptic of the paranormal, and that she found the effect replicable. In one version the writer Eric Wargo adds that her review went beyond Stargate and found overwhelming evidence for psychic ability.
jessica-utts-statistical-analysis-of-cia: The results of Stargate, a long-running US effort backed by the CIA to use psychics as spies, were judged by the statistician Jessica Utts to be far less likely to come from chance than you would expect. Michels brings this up himself, saying the numbers "fall way below" the odds you would expect by luck. If true, it would mean psychic spying showed real effects.
jesus-learned-the-resurrection-technique: Jesus went to Egypt and learned a "resurrection technique" there, according to the writer Whitley Strieber, who says he has met nonhuman beings himself. Strieber offers this as his own reading, drawing on the book Jesus: A New Vision and on the Gospel of Thomas, an ancient collection of sayings attributed to Jesus that is not in the Bible. If he is right, rising from the dead would be a skill Jesus was taught, not a one-off miracle.
jesus-s-return-in-the-first-photograph-o: The writer Whitley Strieber holds that Jesus returned in 1898, when the first photograph was taken of the Shroud of Turin, a linen cloth kept in Turin, Italy, that many believe bears Jesus's image. "That was the moment he returned and we saw him on the shroud," Strieber says, setting out the idea from his book Jesus: A New Vision. If he is right, the second coming would already have happened, through a camera.
jesus-survived-the-crucifixion-in-a-pre-: Jesus did not die on the cross, the story goes, and much more was going on behind the scenes, with the Last Supper a choreographed mystery ritual in which Jesus was sedated and then revived. The researcher Randall Carlson tells it, pointing to the writer Brian Muraresku, author of The Immortality Key, and to Joseph of Arimathea, the man in the Gospels who took Jesus's body. Michels himself, in an earlier episode, frames it as a reading found in some Gnostic, meaning early mystical Christian, interpretations, citing the scholar Elaine Pagels and the Gospels of Thomas, Luke and Matthew.
jet-engine-honda-car-driven-to-los-alamo: Around 1982, a man named Bob Lazar says he took his wife's little Honda, built a jet engine for it from scratch, and drove it, with the car also linked to El Mirage Dry Lake in California and to Los Alamos, New Mexico, home of the nuclear weapons laboratory. Lazar tells it himself during the two days Michels spent with him. It is told as a sign of his hands-on engineering skill.
jets-scrambled-from-santa-cruz-and-anapo: On one night in 1986 that Brazilians call the Night of UFOs, Brazil's air force sent fighter jets up after unknown objects in the sky. Aldo Rebelo, a former Brazilian defense minister, says the jets took off from the Santa Cruz air base in Rio de Janeiro state and the Anápolis air base in Goiás state "in the attempt to intercept the UFOs." Coming from a former defense minister, it amounts to an official confirmation that the military took the sightings seriously.
jewel-beetles-mating-with-stubby-beer-bo: In the Australian outback, male jewel beetles are said to flock to empty stubby beer bottles that people drink, toss out and drive away from, and to try to mate with them. A scientist named Don Hoffman tells this, without naming a source, as an example of how a creature's senses can steer it toward the wrong thing, which bears on his argument that our brains evolved to miss what is really around us.
jfk-and-donald-menzel-s-clearances-1930: Donald Menzel, a Harvard astronomer known as a famous debunker of UFO reports, is said to have quietly held some of the highest security clearances there are, with the CIA (the US spy agency), the NSA (the US code-breaking and eavesdropping agency) and the Navy. Michels tells this himself in three episodes without naming a source. In one he says the young John F. Kennedy, later president, was keen on astrophysics at Harvard and close to Menzel, who admitted the clearances to him. In the others he leaves Kennedy out, and once he calls Menzel a "deep state spook" who was friends with a man named Vannevar Bush. The point is that a leading public skeptic may have been working on the government's side.
jfk-asks-mccone-for-a-full-ufo-briefing-: On June 5, 1963, about five months before his death, President John F. Kennedy is said to have asked to be fully briefed on UFOs. Dan Sheehan, a lawyer and researcher, tells it twice: once he says Kennedy made the request to John McCone, his new CIA director, after pushing the old director, Dulles, into retirement, and once he says the date came from a man named Dick Billings, without naming McCone. It would mean a sitting president was trying to learn what his own spy agency knew about UFOs.
jfk-assassination-linked-to-the-uap-topi: The 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas is tied to the subject of UAPs, the government's term for unidentified flying objects. Jake Barber, a helicopter pilot who says he took part in retrieving such a craft, says this is what he hears the government official Kash Patel saying cryptically in his remarks about the Kennedy files. If true, the assassination would be part of the story of what the government knows about UFOs.
jfk-back-channels-with-khrushchev-and-du: President John F. Kennedy, the story goes, set up secret lines of contact with the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in the 1960s to ease tensions and cut back nuclear weapons, while men inside his own government wanted him gone. Michels frames it this way himself: Kennedy was reaching for détente and denuclearization, and Allen Dulles, the head of the CIA (the US spy agency) whom Kennedy had fired, "basically wanted to take him out." A guest named Dan Sheehan, from an episode titled "The Man Involved In Every American Conspiracy," passes on what he was told by a man named Walter Sullivan. Sheehan says the two leaders exchanged 18 letters "completely secretly outside of the channels of the state department" and outside the CIA, and he ties the Wall Street bank Brown Brothers Harriman to the targeting of Kennedy. If true, it would mean Kennedy's push for peace made him dangerous enemies at home.
jfk-briefed-at-los-alamos-1962: In 1962 President John F. Kennedy is said to have gone to Los Alamos, the government laboratory in New Mexico, to be briefed, a few weeks after some earlier event Michels does not spell out. Michels tells this himself, a little unsure ("I think a couple weeks later"), in an episode with the lawyer Danny Sheehan about Kennedy and UFOs. Michels raises it because it would suggest Kennedy was being told secret things.
jfk-killed-for-ufo-cooperation-breaking-: President John F. Kennedy is said to have been killed in 1963 over the UFO issue. Matthew Pines, a researcher who studies global power, puts it this way: if a leader moved toward disarmament or cooperation with rivals on space and possible UFO technology, it "would cut straight to the core" of a hidden deal among the powerful. Steven Greer, an activist for UFO disclosure, says it is a known fact, that he knows people with "actionable intelligence" on it, and that Kennedy's brother Robert knew. Harald Malmgren, a former presidential adviser who says he handled UFO material, gives his own belief: "I think it was probably the number one issue." Jesse Michels later repeats Malmgren's words in an episode about Joe Rogan. He calls them a kind of deathbed confession from an 89-year-old adviser to Kennedy. If true, it would mean the UFO secret was guarded at the cost of a president's life.
jfk-knew-about-ufos-before-becoming-pres: Harold Malmgren, an economist who advised several US presidents, says John F. Kennedy knew all about UFOs long before he became president in 1961. Malmgren says Kennedy learned it in the 1940s through naval intelligence and the Navy and defense chief James Forrestal, which would mean the subject reached the White House with him.
jfk-letter-to-cia-director-mccone-reques: Ten days before he was killed, President John F. Kennedy is said to have written to the head of the CIA asking for all its data on unexplained objects. The letter is dated November 12, 1963, and is addressed to CIA director John McCone. Jesse Michels says it came out through FOIA, a US law that lets anyone request government records, and he gives the year of release as 2006 at some times and 2005 at others. In his telling, Kennedy asks for "all the data on unknowns" so that the Americans could coordinate with the Soviets, and Michels places it after Kennedy had fired the earlier CIA chief, Allen Dulles. Michels also stresses that its origin is disputed, calling it a letter "of kind of controversial provenance" that should be checked. He credits the records researcher John Greenewald Jr. for it in some tellings. The UFO historian Richard Dolan describes the same memo as Kennedy directing the CIA to share UFO data with the Soviet Union. If it is real, a sitting president was trying to open UFO secrets to a rival power just before his death.
jfk-on-the-harvard-astronomy-department-: In the 1950s, John F. Kennedy, the future president, is said to have sat on the board of overseers, a governing board, for Harvard's astronomy department. The astronomer Beatriz Villarroel tells this from the notes of Stanton Friedman, a UFO researcher. It comes up alongside a story that the Harvard astronomer Donald Menzel was caught destroying photographic plates of the sky, and would tie Kennedy to that department.
jfk-s-planned-ussoviet-alliance-against-: In the 1960s, President John F. Kennedy is said to have planned an alliance with the Soviet Union in which the two countries would go to the moon together and, if needed, jointly "defend the freedom and independence of humanity." The supposed threat was the Nordics, a name in UFO lore for tall, fair, human-looking beings. The researcher Jason Jorjani tells this without naming a source, and he also brings up the president's brother Robert F. Kennedy and the earlier president Dwight Eisenhower. If true, it would mean the Cold War rivals saw a shared enemy that was not human.
jfk-visits-los-alamos-a-month-after-malm: In 1962, the story goes, a young government man named Harold Malmgren, later a presidential adviser, was briefed at Los Alamos, the US nuclear weapons laboratory in New Mexico, and met a man there named Lawrence Preston Gise. Soon afterwards President John F. Kennedy came out to Los Alamos himself. Michels tells it in his own framing, saying the visit came a month after Malmgren's briefing and that it was not really normal for Kennedy to come out and just check on this. Pippa Malmgren, relaying what Harold Malmgren told her, tells it a little differently: she says it was only a couple of weeks later, and that Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson and both men's teams came too. The timing is told as a sign that whatever Malmgren was shown reached the very top.
jfk-wanted-to-declassify-ufo-files-befor: President John F. Kennedy is said to have declared, before his death in 1963, that he wanted to declassify some secret files about aliens and UFOs. Kiran Ilum Xenov, the former president of a Russian republic who says he was himself taken by aliens, tells this as something Kennedy declared, without naming where it was recorded. If true, it would mean a sitting US president meant to reveal the government's UFO secrets.
jim-keller-argues-the-moon-landing-video: A man named Jim Keller is said to argue that the films of the 1969 Moon landing were faked. Michels says that in a debate about whether the Moon landing videos were fake, Keller "takes the fake side." Michels brings it up while asking how much of the official story can be trusted.
jim-lacatski-of-the-dia-part-of-aawsap-w: A rocket scientist named Jim Lacatski, from the Defense Intelligence Agency, the US military's spy agency, took part in AAWSAP, a government programme set up around 2008 to study strange aerial threats, UFOs among them. Michels says Lacatski is now coming out and writing about it. Michels tells this himself and calls it weird, since it means an insider is going public about the programme's work.
jim-marrs-sphere-moves-under-its-own-pow: A metal sphere kept at the Texas home of the late writer Jim Marrs is said to move on its own, with no visible push. The journalist Ross Coulthart says he saw it himself in 2021: "we went to his home and saw this sphere." He also names a man called Patrick Jackson in the story. If it is true, the sphere would be an object driven by some power no one can explain.
jim-penniston-told-the-beings-come-from-: In 1980, in Rendlesham Forest in England, beings are said to have told a witness named Jim Penniston, "we are you, we come from 8,000 years in the future," and that they were having problems reproducing and were taking things from people because of it. A researcher named Mike Masters repeats this, without naming his source, as support for his idea that the visitors are humans from the future. If true, the so-called aliens would be our own distant descendants.
jim-rider-speech-on-devas-fairies-and-th: An executive at Lockheed Martin Space Systems, the space arm of the big American defence company, named Jim Ryder gave a speech in which he talks about devas, fairies and jinn (spirit beings from various traditions), about extrasensory perception, and about "the veil thinning" between worlds. Jesse Michels mentions it himself, saying the speech is available online, as a sign that people deep in the aerospace industry take such ideas seriously.
jim-ryder-s-talk-the-garment-of-god: Michels says a former vice president of Lockheed Martin, the American aerospace and weapons maker, gave a talk called "The Garment of God". The man is named James (Jim) Ryder, and Michels also calls him a director at Skunk Works, the company's secret aircraft design unit. Michels brings up the talk in four episodes and urges everyone to listen to it, since he sees it as a window into how a senior figure in secret aerospace work thinks about deeper questions. His details shift from episode to episode: once he dates it to 2018, once he says Ryder gave it at an event for a spiritual group called the Lucis Trust, and once he calls it "Garment of the Gods" and ties it to Lockheed Martin's space division.
jim-ryder-tried-to-transfer-ufo-to-bigel: In 2008, a man named Jim Ryder from Lockheed Martin Space Systems, part of a large American defence company, is said to have tried to hand over a "UFO" to Bigelow Aerospace, a private space company. Jesse Michels repeats this as something "we now know" from Luis Elizondo, a former Pentagon official who speaks publicly about UFOs, and from others, and links it to a speech Ryder gave. If true, it would mean a defence contractor held a recovered craft and tried to pass it to a private firm.
jim-s-books-documenting-government-funde: A set of books, by an author Tim Gallaudet calls only Jim, is said to fully document strange events studied at Skinwalker Ranch, a property in Utah, during a government-funded research effort from about 2008. Gallaudet, a retired Navy rear admiral, recommends the follow-up book, which he thinks is called Future Visions and New Insights, and says it records the research, the anomalies and the many witnesses. To him it matters because "this is a government funded" study, not a private hobby.
jim-s-pottery-epiphany-and-fixation-on-a: In 1976, an idea about pottery suddenly came to a man named Jim Weiner all at once, and after that he became fixated on ancient sites. Weiner, who appears on the show as a witness in an alien abduction case, tells it from his own life: "all of a sudden this thing came into my head fully developed." He tells it as one of the odd turns in his life that seem to go along with his experiences.
jim-semivan-of-the-cia-briefed-that-psi-: Michels says that people like Jim Semivan, a former officer of the CIA, the US spy agency, have said that psychic powers and the idea that mind and matter are connected, not separate, are "the kind of real core truth. All of that is real." Michels repeats this himself, without naming where it was said, and calls it only tangentially related to UFOs. If true, it would mean insiders believe the mind can act on the physical world.
jim-semivan-opened-the-door-for-mcgwier-: A former CIA officer named Jim Semivan is said to have opened the door for the engineer Bob McGwier to visit Chris Bledsoe, a North Carolina man who says he has had encounters with strange beings and lights and wrote the book UFO of God. McGwier, who made the visit, says Bledsoe told him while he was there that Semivan had said, "oh yeah, you should let Bob in, this should be interesting."
jim-semivan-s-7-hour-briefing-at-the-cia: Jim Semivan, a man who worked at the CIA, is said to have been told by senior officials to book a room inside the agency for six to eight hours so they could give him a briefing that lasted about seven hours. The UFO researcher Grant Cameron passes this on as something Semivan told about. It would mean the CIA holds a large body of UFO knowledge, shared in private with chosen insiders.
jim-semivan-s-bedroom-encounter-with-bei: A man named Jim Semivan says he once stood in his home with his wife while strange beings were there, and someone stood behind him like a guardian: "I was standing there with my wife and these beings were there and there was somebody behind me." The researcher Grant Cameron repeats this as what Semivan described, also naming a person called Ian Dolly. If true, it would be a direct encounter with nonhuman beings in an ordinary bedroom.
jim-semivan-told-ryan-bledsoe-the-family: A man named Jim Semivan is said to have told Ryan Bledsoe, from a family reporting strange experiences, that the family may be part human and part something else. The researcher Jason Simosa says Semivan reportedly told him, "we think you're hybrids," and that the experiences happen because they "may have more non-human DNA." If true, it would explain why one family keeps having these encounters.
jim-semivan-won-t-say-what-is-interestin: Asked what was interesting about Sekret Machines, a novel by the musician Tom DeLonge and the writer A.J. Hartley, a former CIA officer named Jim Semivan flatly said, "No, I'm not going to tell you." The researcher Jason Simosa tells this, apparently from an interview by the podcaster James Iandoli. If it means anything, it hints that the book holds something an insider would not discuss.
jim-simons-nsa-background-and-renaissanc: The mathematician Jim Simons, who founded the secretive and hugely successful investment firm Renaissance Technologies on Long Island, New York, once worked as a codebreaker for the NSA, the US agency that intercepts and breaks foreign communications. The national security analyst Matthew Pines tells Michels this, adding that "there's no such thing as an ex-NSA guy," meaning such ties never really end. In his telling, that background is part of why Renaissance can be seen as a black box whose real workings are hidden.
jimmy-carter-exposes-the-stealth-program: In 1980, while he was running for reelection, President Jimmy Carter is said to have mentioned the stealth program in public. That was the secret effort to build aircraft that radar can't easily see, and the story ties it to Burbank, California. The UFO researcher Grant Cameron tells this without naming a source, as an example of what happens when a leader talks openly about a secret project.
jimmy-carter-s-1969-ufo-sighting: In 1969, before he became US president, Jimmy Carter is said to have seen a UFO. A guest named Dan Sheehan tells it second-hand, saying Carter was with "11 other people" standing "on the steps of this Lion's Club," a local civic club in Georgia, when they saw it. A researcher who goes by the name RedPandaKoala tells it as Carter describing "a bright light" that appeared "in the distance" in the western sky. Michels repeats Sheehan's words on another episode, that Carter "had seen a UFO in 1969." It matters because it would put a future president among those who say they saw something unexplained.
jimmy-carter-s-ufo-briefing-confirmed-by: President Jimmy Carter got a briefing on UFOs in the Oval Office in 1977, and a man named Alonzo McDonald confirmed it, saying he had spoken to the staff who attended and to Carter himself, and that it happened. The scientist Eric W. Davis tells this, repeating what McDonald told him and others in his research group, and points to a June 1977 list of attendees kept by Carter's presidential library. If true, a sitting president was told about UFOs.
jimmy-corsetti-s-theory-that-atlantis-wa: A man named Jimmy Corsetti has put forward the idea that Atlantis, the lost city described by the Greek philosopher Plato, was at the Richat Structure, a giant ring-shaped formation in Mauritania. Michels mentions the theory, linking it to Joe Rogan. The writer Graham Hancock grants that the rings look like Plato's description of Atlantis, but then goes on to qualify the claim. If true, it would place a lost ancient civilisation in the Sahara.
jimmy-savile-at-chequers-and-the-hospita: Jimmy Savile, a famous British television presenter, is said to have been so influential that he spent his Christmases at Chequers, the British prime minister's country house, where the prime minister also spent them. Jay Anderson, a guest on an episode about secret networks of power, passes this on. He tells it to show how close Savile was to the very top of British life.
jimo-borjigin-s-research-on-endogenous-d: A University of Michigan scientist named Jimo Borjigin studies DMT, a psychedelic compound, as the brain may make it on its own, and also terminal lucidity, the sudden clarity some people show just before death. Michels brings this up himself while talking with the neuroscientist Andrew Gallimore, without citing a particular paper, as a sign that science is looking at what happens to the mind at death.
joe-firmage-s-inter-nasa-group: A man named Joe Firmage is said to have started a group called Inter NASA, modeled on the Academy of Arts and Sciences. Michels says so himself, with some hesitation ("I believe"), in an episode with the owner of Skinwalker Ranch, and he does not say what the group did.
joe-mcmoneagle-blind-remote-viewing-of-t: A remote viewer named Joe McMoneagle, one of the people trained to describe faraway places with the mind alone, was given a set of map coordinates without being told what they were, and saw the same mountains, including Mount Perdido in Spain, with the same underground command centres an earlier viewer had described, then saw that the bases were "connected like nodes of a network." Michels tells this himself in an episode about a UFO book the Pentagon tried to censor, without naming any other source. If true, two viewers working blind would have found the same hidden network of bases.
joe-mcmoneagle-remote-views-in-a-scif-ea: The researcher Chris Ramsay says that a remote viewer named Joe McMoneagle would go into a SCIF, a sealed room for handling classified material, and do remote viewing, which means trying to describe distant places or things using only the mind. He did this each year so the budget of Stargate, a US government programme that studied remote viewing, would be renewed. Ramsay tells this without naming a source, and if true it would mean officials kept paying because the demonstrations convinced them.
joe-mcmoneagle-remote-views-the-typhoon-: In 1979 a psychic spy named Joe McMoneagle is said to have used remote viewing, the practice of trying to describe a faraway place with the mind alone, to see a huge new submarine being built at a Soviet shipyard on the White Sea. Paul Smith, who served in the government's psychic spy program, tells this twice on the show as something he heard from McMoneagle. Smith says that "eight months after" the sessions, "the Russians floated out the Typhoon, the biggest submarine ever built", and that details such as where its missile tubes sat matched the sessions. If true, it would show the mind could gather real spy intelligence.
joe-rogan-proposes-weinstein-sit-down-wi: Joe Rogan, host of a very popular podcast, once suggested that the mathematician Eric Weinstein sit down with Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked on alien craft at a secret site in Nevada. Weinstein tells it himself: "Joe once said, 'Let's sit down.'" He brings it up while talking about how claims like Lazar's should be tested in person.
john-alexander-at-romanek-s-house-the-fl: At the Colorado home of Stan Romanek, a man who reports contact experiences, a flashlight is said to have answered questions. According to the story, they went into the backyard, unscrewed the flashlight to the point between on and off, set it on a picnic table, and as Romanek asked questions the flashlight responded by flicking on and off. The UFO researcher Grant Cameron relays it as John B. Alexander, a guest who was there, told it to him.
john-alexander-knew-of-rendlesham-before: A retired US Army colonel named John B. Alexander is said to have known about the Rendlesham incident, a reported UFO encounter in 1980 near a British air base called RAF Woodbridge in England, before almost anyone else in the United States. Jesse Michels says this on three different episodes, once crediting an unnamed well-connected friend and saying Alexander "gave the readout", and elsewhere stating it in his own words, at one point without limiting it to the United States. If true, it would suggest Alexander had unusually early access to secret reports.
john-alexander-s-book-finds-no-majestic-: John B. Alexander, a researcher who looked into UFOs, says in his book on the subject that he never found any group like "Majestic", a secret committee long rumoured to control the UFO matter inside the US government. The philosopher Jason Jorjani sums up the book on the show without quoting it, and also brings up the French UFO researcher Jacques Vallée. It matters because it would mean someone who searched found no sign of the rumoured group.
john-alexander-s-paranormal-research-in-: John B. Alexander, a researcher of the paranormal, is said to have travelled to some 90 or 92 countries studying everything from churches to ceremonies, including those of reindeer herders in Mongolia. Chris Bledsoe, a man who says UFOs appear around him, relays this as what he knows of Alexander. It shows how widely Alexander has looked for strange experiences.
john-alexander-s-telepathic-nordics-at-a: John B. Alexander, a retired Army colonel, is said to have seen Nordics, beings in UFO lore who look like tall, fair, strikingly beautiful humans and talk by telepathy, inside a hotel casino in Las Vegas. The philosopher Jason Jorjani mentions it as one of Alexander's interesting stories. Jesse Michels says Alexander told him the story directly: he saw a couple of these Nordics in the casino, and they looked strikingly beautiful. If true, it would mean such beings walk unnoticed among ordinary people.
john-alexander-sent-to-look-into-the-hut: A man named John Hutchison was said to make objects float in the air, a claimed effect that came to carry his name, and a man named John B. Alexander was given the job of checking it. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, and places Hutchison's work in California. A guest named Nick Cook says he later spoke to Alexander, who told him: "Unfortunately, when I set up all the equipment under laboratory conditions, none of it worked." Cook places the work in Vancouver rather than California. The story matters to the tellers because, if the effect were real, it would mean ordinary objects could be lifted against gravity.
john-aristotle-phillips-atomic-bomb-juni: In 1976 and 1977, a Princeton University student named John Aristotle Phillips wrote his junior thesis, a major paper students write in their third year, on an atomic bomb, and he chose the physicist Freeman Dyson as his advisor for it. The mathematician Eric Weinstein brings this up on the show without naming a source, as an example of how much a single student could work out about bomb design on his own.
john-barrow-s-anti-kardashev-scale-and-o: In the 1990s the cosmologist John Barrow proposed an "anti-Kardashev scale": where the familiar Kardashev scale ranks civilizations by how much energy they command, Barrow's ranks them by how small the things they can engineer are, down to what he called Omega-minus civilizations working at the tiniest scales of reality. The neuroscientist Andrew Gallimore brings this up without naming a source. He uses it to suggest that truly advanced beings might shrink inward rather than spread out across space.
john-dee-s-angelic-work-led-to-colonizin: The English scholar John Dee and his partner Edward Kelley, a medium, are said to have held sessions in which they spoke with angels, and Matthew Brown, a former Pentagon official who presents himself as a whistleblower, tells Michels that this work "led directly to the colonization of the United States of America and the new Atlantis." The New Atlantis here means an ideal new society built in a new land. If true, the founding of America would trace back to messages from unseen beings.
john-dee-s-enochian-angel-language: Michels says that John Dee, a scholar at the court of Queen Elizabeth I of England, served as her chief spy and magician and claimed to speak with angels in what he called the Enochian language. Michels tells this himself on two episodes without naming a source; the second time he describes Dee as a magician who blurred magic and angel contact and does not mention the language. The story matters because it would mean contact with other beings was pursued at the heart of a royal court.
john-ford-s-prosecution-1990: In the 1990s on Long Island, New York, a man named John Ford was prosecuted, and the charges involved a plot, as it is described, to poison someone's toothpaste with radioactive material as part of a move against a governing body. A researcher named Richard Dolan tells this in passing without naming a source, and he also mentions a woman named Elaine Douglas in connection with the case.
john-glenn-s-fireflies-were-ice-crystals: In 1962 the astronaut John Glenn orbited Earth in the capsule Friendship 7 and reported glowing "fireflies" outside, which were really little ice crystals. The researcher and skeptic Michael Shermer mentions it in passing, without naming a source, as an example of a strange sight in the sky that turned out to be ordinary.
john-glenn-urged-harry-reid-to-investiga: The astronaut and senator John Glenn is said to have urged Harry Reid, a powerful senator from Nevada, to look into UFOs, which fed into a government UFO study. Michels mentions this himself in passing in a documentary episode about a former Pentagon official, without naming a source or giving a date.
john-hutchinson-and-the-hutchinson-effec: A man in California named John Hutchison is said to cause what Michels calls the Hutchison effect: metal equipment around him seems to hover in the air and break down. Michels adds that another man, John B. Alexander, "seems to show" up whenever people experience paranormal things like this. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, in an episode about a man he says NASA studies because he attracts UFOs.
john-hutchison-s-lab-in-vancouver-1990: An inventor named John Hutchison is said to have run a cluttered home lab in Vancouver, Canada, from around 1990 to 2009, where he claimed strange effects such as objects lifting off the ground. The aviation journalist Nick Cook says he went there himself and found the home "stuffed full of old oscilloscopes", instruments that show electrical signals on a screen. Cook brings it up in a talk about anti-gravity, where he also mentions an engineer named Boyd Bushman.
john-keel-s-non-government-men-in-black-: Some of the Men in Black, the strange dark-suited visitors said to call on UFO witnesses, were clearly not government agents, according to cases recorded by the writer John Keel in the 1960s. The philosopher Jason Jorjani brings this up from Keel's accounts, without naming a specific book. He uses it to suggest the visitors were something other than human officials.
john-lear-a-billion-aliens-live-in-the-m: In the 1980s, a man named John Lear claimed that aliens were living inside the mountains along a highway, a billion of them going by how the story is titled. A man named Bob Lazar, who knew Lear, repeats it on the show: "he used to tell me there were aliens living in the mountains." If it were true, a huge hidden population would be living right beside an ordinary road.
john-lear-admits-he-made-up-dulce-firefi: A well-known tale says American forces fought a gun battle with aliens in an underground base beneath Archuleta Mesa, near Dulce, New Mexico. According to the writer Greg Bishop, John Lear, a pilot who helped spread the story in the early 1990s, later admitted he invented it, telling Bishop plainly, "Oh yeah, I made that up." Bishop relays this while discussing Paul Bennewitz, a New Mexico man whose ideas fed the Dulce legend. If it is so, one of the most famous parts of that legend would go back to one man's invention.
john-lear-helped-get-bob-lazar-the-s4-jo: Bob Lazar, a man who says he worked on alien craft at S4, a secret site near Area 51 in Nevada, is said to have got that job with help from John Lear, a longtime figure in UFO circles. The researcher UAPGerb says Lear is on record in an interview saying he helped get Lazar the S4 job. Jesse Michels retells it from that interview with more detail. In his version, Lear says a Navy admiral at "MJ level" came to him. Michels explains that MJ in UFO lore means the elite committee said to govern the whole subject. The admiral said they had to "get Bob on the job" because they could hide his role. If true, it would mean Lazar was placed at S4 on purpose by insiders, which would help explain his story.
john-lear-people-live-in-the-sun-1980: A man named John Lear claimed in the 1980s that there are people living in the sun. Bob Lazar, a guest Michels spent two days with, repeats this as something Lear said to him, an example of how far Lear's ideas went.
john-lear-possibly-fed-disinformation-to: A man named Bob Lazar, whose story about secret craft at Area 51, a hidden US test site in the Nevada desert, became famous, may have been fed false information by his close friend John Lear. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, across three episodes. He describes Lear as a pilot who flew cargo planes for the CIA, the US spy agency, in the 1970s and set many flying records. He says it was Lear who leaked Lazar's story to the public, together with the journalist George Knapp and the filmmaker Jeremy Corbell. In one episode Michels adds that Lear had spent a decade hanging around outside Area 51, where the guards knew him by sight. In that episode he goes further and says outright that the CIA pushed the Lazar story out. If true, this would mean Lazar's account was shaped by an intelligence agency. All three tellings come from Michels alone, and they differ only in how far he takes the idea.
john-lear-s-1977-lake-level-photos-of-gr: A pilot named John Lear is said to have had original photographs from 1977, taken at ground level at Groom Lake, the dry lakebed in Nevada where the secret base known as Area 51 sits, showing a chain stretched across. The story also involves the film being swapped. The filmmaker Jeremy Corbell tells it as something Lear told him, and if true it would mean early pictures of the base existed before they were taken out of circulation.
john-lear-s-area-51-access-and-the-f-117: Michels says that John Lear, a pilot with access to Area 51, a secret US Air Force test base in Nevada, leaked details of the F-117, a stealth attack jet kept secret during the 1980s, to the Las Vegas TV journalist George Knapp. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source. It matters because it would show Lear really had inside knowledge of the base.
john-lear-the-moon-was-built-at-jupiter-: The moon, so the story goes, was built at Jupiter, made there like a product, and then towed into orbit around Earth. Bob Lazar, a man who says he once worked on recovered alien craft for the US government, tells Michels this is what a veteran pilot named John Lear told him. If it were true, the moon would be a made object that someone placed next to Earth on purpose.
john-lilly-s-contact-with-ecco-and-solid: The scientist John Lilly, who invented the isolation tank, a dark, silent tank of salt water for floating cut off from the senses, claimed to be in contact with two non-human intelligences. Michels tells this several times from what Lilly wrote, including Lilly's book Programming and Metaprogramming in the Human Biocomputer: one being, called the solid state intelligence, said it was trying to appear on Earth and needed more silicon to do it, while the other was something Michels half remembers as ECCO, the Earth coincidence control mechanism, and on one telling he calls Lilly a CIA scientist working from the 1950s to the 1970s. He raises it because, if true, it would suggest an alien mind tied to computers and silicon.
john-mack-and-terence-mckenna-on-the-wes: A man named John Mack is said to have predicted that the Western way of seeing the world would "burst open", and that people would come to see it as "incredibly myopic and closed". Michels tells this himself without naming a source. He sets it beside the thinker Terence McKenna and the historian of science Thomas Kuhn, who wrote about how big scientific worldviews collapse and get replaced. If they are right, our whole picture of reality is about to change.
john-mack-at-harvard-his-friend-bud-hopk: In the 1990s, Jesse Michels says, a psychiatrist named John Mack headed the psychiatry department at Harvard and had been friends since childhood with a man named Budd Hopkins. Michels brings this up himself, without naming a source, while talking with a neuroscientist about strange experiences. The story is linked to the thinker Thomas Kuhn and some advice he gave, but Michels does not say what that advice was. It matters to him because it puts a senior Harvard psychiatrist close to the study of people who say they were taken by aliens.
john-mack-moves-away-from-a-physical-exp: The Harvard psychiatrist John Mack, who studied people who said they had been taken by aliens, became over the years "less convinced that this was a purely physical nuts and bolts phenomenon," according to the neuroscientist Andrew Gallimore. Gallimore, who studies the psychedelic drug DMT, tells Michels this alongside the work of Rick Strassman, a psychiatrist who gave DMT to volunteers. He raises it because it suggests abductions may happen in some realm of the mind rather than in physical spacecraft.
john-mack-persecuted-by-harvard-over-his: A Harvard researcher named John Mack, who studied people reporting abduction by aliens, was persecuted by Harvard University for that work in the 1990s, and there was even a trial there. Michels says this himself, in passing, without naming a source. If it is true, a major university put one of its own on trial for taking abduction reports seriously.
john-mack-s-abductee-interviews-at-harva: In the 1990s, a Harvard psychiatrist named John Mack began listening to people who said aliens had taken them, and he looked into these abduction accounts on a personal, story-by-story level. Michels tells this himself on two episodes, without naming a source. In 2022 he calls Mack the head of Harvard's psychiatry department. In 2023 he describes him instead as a private clinician whose patients brought up alien encounters on their own, and he mentions the philosopher of science Thomas Kuhn alongside him.
john-mack-s-abductee-research-judged-too: In the 1990s at Harvard, John Mack studied people who said they had been taken by aliens. The skeptic Michael Shermer says of him, "I think he was a little too open-minded." Shermer's point is that Mack accepted his subjects' accounts too readily, and he offers it as his own judgment, naming no source.
john-mack-s-abductees-and-the-double-ide: People who say aliens took them often start in terror, the "ontological shock" of seeing a gray being, the small grey-skinned figure of abduction stories, in their bedroom, but over time many come to identify with the being. Michels passes this on as something said by John Mack, a psychiatrist who studied people reporting alien abductions, and he puts it to Jeffrey Mishlove, a researcher with a doctorate in parapsychology, saying Mack went "one step deeper" on it with him. If so, the experience would reshape a person's sense of who they are, not just frighten them.
john-mack-s-abduction-cases-were-done-by: In the 1990s John Mack, a Harvard figure who studied people who said aliens had abducted them, was sent a stream of cases, and every one of them was really "done by humans." The UFO researcher Steven Greer says this without naming a source, and he also brings up Budd Hopkins, another abduction researcher. If true, it would mean someone staged these abductions and fed them to the researchers on purpose.
john-mack-s-death-in-a-car-crash-sheehan: The psychiatrist John Mack was killed in 2004 when a car ran him down, and a lawyer named Dan Sheehan says he looked into the death within hours of it happening. Sheehan says he dug into it and found out who the driver was, a man he says is still in prison and who, by his account, "was just drunk". That answers, in his view, the question of whether there was anything more behind the death.
john-mack-s-experiencer-support-group-an: The people in a support group for those who say they were taken by aliens, run in the Boston area by the psychiatrist John Mack, split into two different camps, according to Jim Weiner. Weiner, who appears on the show as an abduction witness, says he went to the groups himself and noticed this division, though he does not spell out here what set the two camps apart. His point is that the people reporting these experiences do not all see them the same way.
john-mack-s-final-manuscript-when-worldv: John Mack, a Harvard psychiatrist, left a last manuscript called When Worldviews Collide, which he wrote in the early 2000s, between about 2000 and 2003. A lawyer named Danny Sheehan, who says he knew the work at first hand, gives its title on the show: "actually the name of his manuscript is When Worldviews Collide." He brings it up because it would show what Mack was trying to say at the end of his career.
john-mack-s-harvard-study-of-alien-abduc: John Mack, head of the psychiatry department at Harvard University, spent the last part of his career in the 1990s studying people who said they had been taken by aliens, recovering their memories with hypnosis and holotropic breathwork, a deep, fast breathing method. Michels tells this himself in three episodes, twice adding that Mack was friends with Thomas Kuhn, the thinker behind the book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions about how science changes, and once naming Mack's methods without mentioning Kuhn. He tells it to show a leading scientist taking the subject seriously.
john-mack-s-personal-quest-behind-his-ab: The Harvard psychiatrist John Mack, who in the 1990s studied people who said they had been taken by aliens, is said to have been driven by a personal spiritual search, shaped in part by the psychiatrist Stanislav Grof. Michels brings this up from The Believer, a book about Mack by the journalist Ralph Blumenthal, which he calls amazing. If true, it would mean Mack's abduction work grew out of his own inner quest as much as out of his patients.
john-mccarthy-s-bureau-of-simulation-sto: John McCarthy, the computer scientist who ran the artificial intelligence lab at Stanford, used to tell a story in which a man one day gets a letter from the "Bureau of Simulation" that begins "Dear Sir". The computer scientist and UFO researcher Jacques Vallée tells it twice, as a story he heard McCarthy tell around 1968. In his second telling Vallée adds that the story is about replacing a man who has become predictable, the point being that a life easy enough to predict could be run by a simulation.
john-mcdowell-s-forensic-assessment-of-t: The small three-fingered bodies found in Peru may, by some evidence, have once been living creatures, says the forensic investigator John McDowell, who examined them. McDowell says there is data to show that some of these bodies can be read as perhaps living organisms, which would mean they are not simply made objects. Jesse Michels adds that McDowell saw the bodies in person, together with Jim Caruso, the chief medical examiner for Denver and a forensic pathologist.
john-mills-sees-ufos-at-malmstrom-1990: In the early 1990s a retired missile technician named John Mills saw a lot of UFOs at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, a base that holds nuclear missiles. Michels mentions it himself in passing, without naming a source, as one of several reports linking UFOs to nuclear weapons sites.
john-mills-sees-zigzagging-object-near-m: In January 1993, according to Jesse Michels, a missile crew member named John Mills was driving with a six-person crew back to Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, a base that holds nuclear missiles, when he saw a bright object zigzagging across the sky. Michels tells it more than once, in conversations with the researcher Robert Hastings and the former Air Force officer Robert Salas, and on one telling adds that when Mills got back, officers told him the base had been swarmed by unidentified objects. Another telling leaves out the zigzagging and mentions only the swarming. Michels tells it as one more case of strange objects showing up around nuclear weapons sites.
john-mulholland-trained-the-cia-in-decep: A man named John Mulholland trained the CIA, the US spy agency, in deception and trickery in the 1950s and wrote a manual on how to do it. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, as a sign of how seriously the agency took the craft of misleading people in that era.
john-norseen-at-allagash-during-1976-abd: A man named John Norseen is said to have been at Allagash, a remote area of Maine, in 1976, when a group of people there say they were abducted. He was supposedly testing a tracking device that goes under the skin. An unnamed witness to that abduction says Norseen told him so himself: "he was doing a TTR, tag, trace, retrieve exercise with a subcutaneous device that they were testing." If true, at least part of the abduction would have involved humans testing tracking technology.
john-norseen-s-biofusion-thought-control: In 1999 a researcher at the defense company Lockheed Martin named John Norseen wrote a report on "biofusion", a system he later described as linking brains to computers so a pilot's thoughts could become commands in the cockpit. The report was called Biofusion Reflexive Control and Neuro-ergonomic Integration in Adaptive Cockpits. Michels tells this himself in an episode about a UFO book the Pentagon tried to censor, as a sign that the military was working on mind-controlled machines.
john-norsine-s-patent-for-piloting-a-cra: An engineer named John Norsine is said to hold a locked patent, meaning one sealed from public view, for what Michels calls "essentially how to fly a UFO with your mind." Michels tells this himself, and in a later episode he adds that the patents, which he links to the aircraft maker Lockheed, involve "neural imprints and neural interfaces," links between the brain and a machine, for flying aircraft. He also mentions a study on the same idea by the research organisation Battelle, which he thinks came out in the early 2020s. If it is true, someone has worked out how to pilot a craft by thought alone.
john-p-craven-s-the-silent-war-on-retrie: A book called The Silent War, by a senior Navy figure named John Piña Craven, is said to describe the US Navy secretly recovering exotic technology from the seafloor. Michels brings it up himself on several episodes, sometimes saying the recoveries were made by submarines and sometimes speaking more broadly of covert operations to find things on the sea floor. Once he also names a second book, Blind Man's Bluff, and calls Craven one of the godfathers of the Navy's seafloor recovery work, which would mean the military has long pulled strange objects out of the ocean.
john-paul-and-episode-9-as-proof-of-an-a: A filmmaker named Ky Dickens, who made a documentary series called The Telepathy Tapes about children said to read minds, says that someone named John Paul gave her what she took as proof of an afterlife. She tells it first-hand on Michels's show, tying it to episode 9 of her series and to time spent in Atlanta, Georgia, around 2024. If true, it would mean some part of a person goes on after death.
john-paul-and-lily-go-on-telepathic-date: Two young people named John Paul and Lily go on "dates" in Atlanta in 2023 while staying on different floors of a house, and they communicate by telepathy, meaning mind to mind, without speaking. The filmmaker Ky Dickens, who made a documentary about nonverbal autistic people said to be telepathic, relays this from what she was told, including by a woman named Libby. If true, it would mean these two can talk across a house with no words at all.
john-paul-ii-establishes-vatican-observa: In the late 1980s Pope John Paul II is said to have signed a decree setting up a special observatory inside the Vatican to study UFOs. A guest named Kiran Ilum Xenov, introduced as the president of a Russian republic, says this, passing it on as something he had heard: "The pope signed a decree and a special observatory was established right there inside the Vatican." If true, it would mean the Catholic Church quietly took UFOs seriously enough to watch for them.
john-peterson-s-1998-arlington-institute: In 1998, John Peterson, head of the Arlington Institute, a think tank, is said to have invited people to a small private conference about what the world would be like if extraterrestrials were openly acknowledged as living among us. The UFO historian Richard Dolan relays this as told by Katherine Austin Fitz, who was invited. If true, it would suggest some insiders were planning for open contact.
john-ramirez-on-human-alien-hybrid-progr: A former CIA officer named John Ramirez, who reached GS-15, one of the top grades in the US civil service, has said publicly that he is sure the United States runs programmes breeding human and alien hybrids. Jesse Michels repeats this, saying Ramirez has come forward with it, and mentions it alongside Luis Elizondo, a former Pentagon official who led a small office studying unexplained aerial reports.
john-ramirez-says-everyone-is-waiting-fo: In 2022, a former intelligence officer named John Ramirez said, more or less, that everyone is waiting for Luis Elizondo to talk about hybrids, meaning beings that are part human and part something else. Elizondo is a former official linked to a small Pentagon office that studied unexplained aerial reports. A researcher named Jason Simosa repeats Ramirez's remark to Michels, as a hint that insiders know about such beings and that Elizondo might one day say so.
john-trump-examines-tesla-s-confiscated-: When the inventor Nikola Tesla died in 1943, the story goes, the FBI, the US federal police, seized his papers, and an engineer named John G. Trump was sent to go through them. Michels tells it again and again on the show, in his own words and without naming a source. He describes Trump as a professor at MIT, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, "the country's leading radar expert at the time, and Donald Trump's uncle." According to Michels, the FBI raided Tesla's apartment by Bryant Park in New York, and the files "were seized and put in a vault." Trump's job was to see whether anything in them "would be of service to national security," or would "confer any tactical warfare advantages to the United States." Michels also says the researcher Bill Moore interviewed Trump for a documentary about the Philadelphia Experiment, a story of a secret wartime Navy experiment. A researcher who goes by RedPandaKoala tells it more simply: Trump was so clever that when Tesla died the government called on him to "go through like all of his notes." One of Michels's tellings dates it loosely to the 1940s instead of 1943. It is told because it would mean Tesla's work was treated as a possible military secret.
john-trump-likely-involved-in-the-1952-w: A man named John G. Trump was probably involved in the 1952 wave, a run of UFO sightings over Washington, D.C. that showed up heavily on radar. A researcher who goes by RedPandaKoala offers this as a personal guess, in an episode about UFOs and nuclear weapons, saying "I personally think he would have been involved" because it was "a very radar-intensive wave." If so, it would tie a known figure to the government's handling of those sightings.
john-wheeler-s-u-diagram-of-the-self-obs: The physicist John Wheeler drew the universe as a letter U: one tip is the Big Bang, and the other tip is an eyeball staring back at the Big Bang, so the universe looks back at its own beginning. The writer Eric Wargo describes the drawing in his own summary, linking it to the physicists Yakir Aharonov and John Cramer. The idea he draws from it is that observers now might help shape the universe's past.
johns-hopkins-president-rumored-on-mj-12: Jesse Michels says that a scientist named Detlev Bronk, who was president of Johns Hopkins University, is rumored to have sat on "Majestic 12", said to be a secret group set up to handle crashed alien craft. He says Bronk is also rumored to have done autopsies on the bodies of "non-human intelligence", meaning beings that are not human. Michels passes this on himself as a rumor, without naming a source. If true, it would mean a leading American scientist examined alien bodies in secret.
johnson-s-first-meeting-after-kecksburg-: After an object reportedly fell from the sky at Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, in 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson's first meeting on his return to the White House was said to be with the head of the federal emergency management office. The Canadian UFO researcher Grant Cameron tells Michels this, referring to it as something on record, though he does not quote the document. He brings it up because such a meeting would suggest the government treated the Kecksburg event as a serious emergency.
johnson-space-center-as-likely-home-of-a: A secret crewed space program, one that would move people and supplies through space, might be run out of NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA is the US space agency, and Johnson is its base for human spaceflight. Michels raises this himself, in his own framing. His reason is that this is the same center where a hacker named Gary McKinnon says he found UFO-related images and spreadsheets. If that were true, a hidden program would be sitting inside a well-known public agency.
johnston-island-scuttlebutt-soviet-orbit: Around 1962, on Johnston Island, a tiny Pacific atoll used for American nuclear tests, the story went that the Soviets had put a nuclear weapon into orbit, President Kennedy told the Soviet leader Khrushchev to take it down, and an explosion lit up the whole South Pacific, sparking UFO reports, after which something fell toward the island and was recovered. A man named Bob Jacobs tells this as what he and others were told, framing the talk of a UFO shootdown as cover for the Soviet nuke, and Michels repeats Jacobs's account of the fallen object being recovered.
joining-skywatcher-to-lead-psionic-opera: A man named Jordan Jose says that in 2024 he chose to join Skywatcher, a private company that tries to call UFOs into view, and to lead its "psionic" work, meaning the use of mind powers such as telepathy to make contact. He tells this as his own story, naming Jake Barber, James Fer and a colleague he calls Alex as part of the team. If true, it means a company was openly using trained minds as a tool to summon unknown craft.
joining-the-project-in-1978-by-1979-no-d: Joe McMoneagle, a former Army remote viewer, says the military's remote viewing project at Fort Meade, Maryland, brought him in in October 1978. Remote viewing is the claimed ability to describe faraway places or things using only the mind. He says that by July 1979 the team knew "there was no defense against" it, which would mean no secret anywhere could be fully protected from such spying.
joint-chiefs-propose-operation-northwood: In 1962 the Joint Chiefs, the heads of the US armed forces, are said to have put a plan called Operation Northwoods in front of the president. A researcher named Dan Sheehan brings it up only in passing, without naming a source, and links it to the Air Force general Curtis LeMay, as part of his account of the pressures President John F. Kennedy faced.
joint-chiefs-staff-colonel-confirms-a-uf: In the 1980s in Washington, a colonel working for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the group of top military commanders who advise the president, said yes when asked straight out whether there was really a UFO cover-up. The physicist John Brandenburg says he asked the question himself, and that the colonel answered: "Yes. That's all I can tell you. The rest you can figure out for yourself." Brandenburg tells it as a rare moment of an insider admitting that the government hides what it knows.
joint-stars-synthetic-aperture-radar-pro: A doctor who worked with NASA named Greg Rogers says that Joint Stars, a military aircraft programme built around synthetic aperture radar, a radar that makes detailed images of the ground, proved itself in Desert Storm, the 1991 US-led war against Iraq. Rogers, who says he was part of this world, says that after that, the military decided it would never go into combat again without this radar. He tells it to show how a secret technology can quietly become essential.
jolly-west-mk-ultra-and-cult-creation-19: The psychiatrist Jolly West, longtime head of psychiatry at the University of California, Los Angeles, is said to have been one of the architects of MK Ultra, a secret CIA program of mind-control experiments, and to have exchanged letters with Sidney Gottlieb, the CIA chemist behind it. Jesse Michels tells this across three episodes, drawing on the psychiatrist Colin Ross's book CIA Doctors and the journalist Tom O'Neill's book Chaos, and he goes further to suggest West was probably using such methods on the cult leader Charles Manson. If true, it would tie a government mind-control program to the making of a cult.
jolly-west-s-mk-ultra-violence-creation-: Michels suggests that in 1960s California, a psychiatrist named Jolly West, working within MK Ultra, the CIA's secret mind-control research programme, may have stirred up local violence, such as that linked to the cult leader Charles Manson, to frighten the wider public into calm. This is Michels's own theory, offered with an "I kind of think" and without naming a source. If it were true, it would mean violence was manufactured on purpose to keep a whole population docile.
jonathan-weygandt-and-the-crashed-craft-: Jonathan Weygandt, a Marine lance corporal, says he came across a crashed craft not made by humans in the jungle of Peru. He tells it himself, showing his own drawing of the craft "embedded in the rock." UAPGerb, an online UFO researcher who documented the case, dates it to 1997. He says Weygandt was serving in Operation Laser Strike, an anti-drug mission, when his unit found an enormous egg- or teardrop-shaped craft lodged in a cliff face. In UAPGerb's account, men in Department of Energy rain jackets took Weygandt and flew him in a CH-47, a large military helicopter, to an obscure base. There he says Chinese and German personnel worked alongside Americans, and he was questioned for days. The filmmaker James Fox adds that Weygandt saw green liquid dripping from the craft, and the case is also credited to the disclosure activist Steven Greer and a researcher named Dan Willis. The story's own dating puts it in the early 1990s, while the tellers say 1997. If true, it would mean crash retrieval is an international operation that holds witnesses by force.
jordan-from-sonica-predicts-the-next-day: During a 2025 field operation by Skywatcher, a company that tries to call UFOs into view, its lead mind-powers specialist, Jordan Jose, is said to have predicted the next day's events: "Hey, tomorrow we will see conflict in the sky." James Valor, one of the company's leaders, tells it as something he witnessed, saying Jose came up to him and a colleague named Alex with the warning. If true, it suggests the team could foresee what would appear in the sky.
jordan-of-skywatchers-shown-a-sphere-in-: A man named Jordan Jose, connected to a group called Skywatchers, is said to have been taken into something called the GATE program as a late teenager, where military officers, intelligence people and scientists brought in a case, opened it, and showed him a sphere exactly like one seen elsewhere. The researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb tells this as something Jose told him, and it would mean officials have long held such spheres and shown them to chosen young people.
jordan-psionically-calls-in-an-egg-objec: In August 2024, at an event site with a patio and backyard, one of Skywatcher's main "psi-actives", a man named Jordan Jose, is said to have used his mind to call in an object that may have been shaped like an "egg", and a man named Fred Baker filmed it. Skywatcher is a startup that tries to summon UFOs, and "psi-actives" is its word for people it says have psychic abilities. A witness speaking for the company tells it as an example of their work, saying Jordan "probably caused" the object, and admits they don't know what it was.
jordan-s-gifted-program-childhood-and-sk: A witness named Jordan Jose has spoken about being put in gifted programs as a child and working on secret programs, which the title ties to something called Sky Watcher that the telling does not describe. A guest who goes by the online name UAPGerb, himself a witness, says Jordan is the only person he knows who has talked about this, and he names no other source. If true, it would mean children were picked out and trained for hidden projects.
jordan-s-mri-shows-dense-white-matter-in: A brain scan of a man named Jordan Jose shows unusually dense white matter in the caudate and putamen, two structures deep inside the brain, according to Jose himself. Jose, who says he was taken into a secret UFO program as a child, links this to research by the scientist Garry Nolan and says he has "a very unique caudate and putamen." If true, it would mean his experiences left a mark that a scanner can measure.
jorjani-invited-to-join-the-knights-of-m: The philosopher Jason Jorjani says he was once invited to join the Knights of Malta, an old Catholic order of knights, through an initiation ritual held on the island of Malta. He tells it as something that happened to him, mentioning it in passing: "I was invited, by the way, to join the Knights of Malta at one point."
jorjani-s-dinner-with-jacques-vallee-on-: The philosopher Jason Jorjani says that around 2016 or 2017 the veteran UFO researcher Jacques Vallée invited him to his home for dinner, where the two had "a fairly intimate conversation" and Jorjani put to him a question about time travel. Jorjani tells it as his own memory. It matters to him because it would show a leading figure in the field taking the idea of time travel seriously in private.
jorjani-s-great-aunt-talking-with-dead-r: The philosopher Jason Jorjani says that his great aunt, as she lay dying in a hospital room, was not just describing her dead relatives but actually having conversations with them. Jorjani was there and tells it as a case he saw himself, the kind that would suggest the dying can reach the dead.
jorjani-s-persian-grandmother-talking-to: As she lay dying, the Persian grandmother of the writer and researcher Jason Jorjani began talking to his grandfather, who had been dead for a long time. Jorjani tells it as something he saw in his own family: "She starts talking to my dead grandfather." He offers it as a personal example of the dying seeming to make contact with the dead.
