He makes the point himself on a 2025 episode with the UFO activist Steven Greer. He uses it to argue that big tech companies and the government work closely together in keeping secrets.
society-for-psychical-research-and-the-h: Scientific studies of psychic powers such as telepathy have been going on since the 1870s, starting with the Society for Psychical Research, a group set up to test such claims, and figures like the writer Frederick Myers and the psychologist William James. A documentary maker named Ky Dickens says this to show that her own work on telepathy has a long history behind it. She names no particular source.
socorro-footprints-and-hynek-s-conversio: In 1964 there were footprints on the ground at Socorro, New Mexico, after a reported UFO landing, and seeing them is what changed the mind of J. Allen Hynek, the astronomer who advised the US Air Force on UFO reports. This comes from John Blitch, a former scientist at the Pentagon's advanced research agency, who tells it to Michels in passing without naming a source. In his telling, it is the moment a leading skeptic started taking the subject seriously.
solar-camera-aimed-at-the-portal-spot-on: On Bradshaw Ranch near Sedona, Arizona, a fenced-off property, a camera powered by solar panels is aimed at one exact spot: the place where Linda Bradshaw, who lived on the ranch, says she saw a portal, a doorway into somewhere else. The journalist Ross Coulthart tells Michels he saw the camera himself in 2025, pointing "exactly at the point where Linda Bradshaw says she saw the portal." He takes it to mean that someone is still watching the spot closely.
soldiers-and-officers-confirm-the-giant-: A handful of soldiers and officers have told Tim Alberino, a guest who says US forces captured a 12-foot giant in Afghanistan, that the story is true. They also told him there are even wilder stories and more giants out there than just the one. Alberino repeats what these people told him without naming them, and if they are right, the giant would not be a one-off.
solon-brown-weeps-telling-deacon-bruce-s: In 1948 near Aztec, New Mexico, a man named Solon Brown broke down and cried while telling a church deacon named Bruce Seer about what he had seen, in the setting of a reported saucer crash there. Michels tells it in an episode about that crash, drawing on the researcher Scott Ramsey. Sixty years later, Seer's son told Ramsey he never forgot that night, because it was the first time he had ever seen a grown man cry.
solon-told-the-atlantis-story-by-priests: The Athenian lawgiver Solon is said to have learned the story of Atlantis, a lost island power, from Egyptian priests at the temple of the goddess Neith in Sais, a city in the Nile Delta. The writer Graham Hancock tells Michels this twice, drawing on Plato's dialogues the Timaeus and the Critias, read here in Benjamin Jowett's translation; in one telling he adds that the priests read hieroglyphs off the temple wall and translated them for Solon, and he dates the visit to about 600 BC and the events to about 9600 BC. The researcher Tim Alberino recalls the same scene to stress what the priest taught about cycles of catastrophe, which he ties to our own age. In Plato's text Solon is "received there with great honour," and an aged priest tells him: "O Solon, Solon, you Hellenes are never anything but children." The priest says great deeds "have all been written down by us of old, and are preserved in our temples," with particulars in "the sacred registers themselves"; the text does not say they were carved on the temple wall or read aloud from hieroglyphs. Critias also says that the Egyptians had translated the names into their own tongue and that Solon translated them back. If true, it would mean Egypt kept records of a civilisation far older than the Greeks knew.
something-above-the-ranch-defies-rockets: Something in the sky over Skinwalker Ranch, a Utah property known for reports of strange events, interferes with rockets and drones, and something odd lies under the ground too, says Brandon Fugal, the ranch's owner. Fugal says his team has recorded this since about 2016: "there is something within the space above the ranch that defies rockets, that manipulates drones." He tells it as what his own research there has found.
something-showed-up-in-the-mid-2000s-tha: Something appeared around the middle of the 2000s that the United States was not tracking, and it changed the game. That is the view of a guest named Dylan Borland, who says a top government official once told him that aliens run everything, and he offers it to Jesse Michels as his own belief rather than a described event. If he is right, the government's handling of the subject would have shifted around that time.
son-of-man-title-taken-from-the-parables: The title "son of man" that Jesus of Nazareth uses for himself comes from the Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish text left out of most Bibles, says a researcher named Tim Alberino. He gives no source but points to its second section, called the Parables: "The proper title the son of man comes from first Enoch specifically from the second section of first Enoch which is called the parables." He also mentions the Book of Daniel. If he is right, it would tie Jesus's view of himself to Enoch's stories.
sonny-white-at-nasa-eagleworks-claims-ca: An engineer named Harold "Sonny" White, who worked at NASA Eagleworks, a small NASA lab for unusual propulsion ideas, is said to claim he can power a 1.5 kilovolt microchip using the Casimir effect, a tiny force that appears between objects placed very close together in empty space. Michels tells this himself, passing on White's claim, in an episode with a former director of the NSA, the US agency for electronic intelligence. If true, it would mean usable power can be drawn from empty space.
sonny-white-harnessing-the-casimir-force: An engineer named Harold "Sonny" White seems to be harnessing the Casimir force, a tiny push between very close surfaces that physicists say comes from empty space itself, on small scales. Michels says this himself, without naming a source, during a debate with a skeptic in 2026. He raises it as a sign that people are already learning to tap energy from the vacuum, the kind of physics some link to UFO propulsion.
sonny-white-s-casimir-effect-chip: A researcher named Harold "Sonny" White can, in Jesse Michels's words, "engineer the Casimir effect". The Casimir effect is a tiny force that pulls two very close surfaces together, and it comes from empty space itself. Michels says this himself, in passing and without naming a source, as one example of people working toward exotic physics, presumably on a chip.
sonny-white-s-nasa-eagleworks-warp-drive: A NASA researcher named Harold "Sonny" White worked on a warp drive, a way of moving a craft by bending space itself, at a small NASA lab called Eagleworks, sometime between about 2010 and 2019. Michels brings this up himself, without naming a source, and adds that he thinks White is now funded by DARPA, the Pentagon's agency for advanced research, through a company called "Limitless or something like that." If so, it would mean the military is backing serious work on faster-than-light travel.
sound-light-and-frequency-formula-writte: On September 21, 1996, in the Los Angeles backyard of the television writer Bryce Zabel, a man known as JC scribbled a formula on an ATM deposit envelope in about 30 seconds and told the screenwriter Brent Friedman to keep it in a safety deposit box for 10 to 15 years, saying that if they never made a deal, "you'll know I was for real." Friedman, who was there and says Zabel was too, says it looked like an incomprehensible formula, and when he asked what it was, JC answered: "sound, light and frequency, secrets of the universe." If true, a stranger handed Hollywood writers what he claimed was a key to how the universe works.
sound-light-and-frequency-turns-up-in-a-: The phrase "sound, light and frequency" turned up word for word in a 2012 white paper from CERN, the European physics laboratory, about turning the data from the discovery of the so-called God particle into sound, says the screenwriter Brent Friedman. Friedman says he had used the phrase himself and searched for it, and that this was the first hit he got, about fifteen years later. He tells it as a strange echo between his own work and frontier physics.
source-visibly-shaking-while-briefing-se: Some people who came to brief US Senate staff on what they knew about UFOs were so nervous that they shook, according to Kurt McConnell, a Senate staffer who sat in on those briefings on Capitol Hill from around 2017. He tells Michels he recalls one source who "was visibly shaking" as they began to explain what they knew. In a later episode, prompted by Michels, he speaks more broadly of sources who were "extremely earnest," had "credible backgrounds," and were "nervous and they're shaking." He tells it as a sign that these people believed what they were saying and felt it was risky to say it.
source-who-has-been-inside-s4: S4 is said to be a secret site near Papoose Lake in Nevada, close to the base known as Area 51. A UFO researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb says he has talked with one person who has been inside S4. He does not name that person or say what they saw, but if true it would mean the site is real and people have worked there.
sources-tell-senators-of-recovered-and-r: Between 2017 and 2024, people came to Capitol Hill and told senators that the government had recovered craft not made by humans and taken them apart to learn how they work. Kurt McConnell, a staffer for the US Senate, says he was there, and that these people "met with senators" and "made precisely those kinds of claims." If true, it would mean such programs exist and were reported to Congress.
southcom-tic-tac-detected-by-space-asset: Somewhere at sea in the area covered by Southern Command, the US military command responsible for Central and South America, a "tic tac", a white oval object shaped like the mint, was reportedly picked up by a sensor in space close to a Navy ship. Michels reads the line himself from a report called Immaculate Constellation, which comes through Matthew Brown, described in the episode as a Pentagon whistleblower: "tic tac detected by space asset in proximity of vessel." If true, it would mean the military tracked such objects from space as well as from ships and planes.
southwest-research-analysis-of-the-impla: In the mid-1990s, a sliver of what the writer Whitley Strieber calls an implant from his body was examined at the Southwest Research Institute, a research lab in San Antonio, Texas. Strieber says a man named Bill, William Malow, called to say he had the piece and that it had a metal base with tiny moving hair-like strands, which he called cilia, coming off it. Strieber tells it second-hand, as what Malow told him, and it would mean the object was something no ordinary metal fragment could explain.
soviet-divers-meet-tall-humanoids-at-lak: In 1982, the story goes, Soviet divers went down into Lake Baikal, a lake in the Soviet Union, to look for something and came face to face with very tall humanlike beings, an encounter that seems to have left them badly shaken. Michels raises it himself as a question to his guest, a treasure hunter named Dennis Asberg, without naming a source, and he breaks off before finishing it. If true, it would place strange beings deep underwater, far from where anyone expects them.
soviet-horten-based-flying-saucer-progra: After the Second World War the Soviet Union ran a program to build a kind of flying saucer, based on the designs of the Horten brothers, German aircraft makers, according to the author Peter Levenda. He says this came out when the Soviet Union fell and some of its documentation became available, though he does not name the papers. If true, it would mean saucer-shaped craft were a human engineering project on both sides of the Cold War.
soviet-microwave-beaming-of-the-us-embas: In the 1970s, the Soviets beamed microwaves at the US embassy in Moscow, and Henry Kissinger, the American statesman, told them to stop. Michels tells this himself, crediting reporting by the German magazine Der Spiegel and the TV news show 60 Minutes, and says he thinks it came up around 1976 during the SALT talks, the arms limitation negotiations between the US and the Soviet Union, when Kissinger told the Soviet diplomat Anatoly Dobrynin to "stop beaming our embassy with microwaves." If so, it would show both superpowers already knew of energy weapons aimed at people decades ago.
soviet-military-exercise-drew-ufos-once-: During the Soviet era, a military exercise was set up on purpose to try to attract UFOs, and the story goes that they turned up once nuclear weapons were brought in. Robert Hastings, a researcher who studies UFO reports at nuclear weapons sites, passes this on from a retired Soviet army colonel whom he does not name, and he says the colonel tells it himself in a video on the internet. Hastings tells it because, if true, it would mean UFOs are drawn to nuclear weapons outside the United States too.
soviet-missiles-brought-online-1960: In the 1960s, nuclear missiles in the Soviet Union are said to have been switched on by themselves while unidentified objects were present, much like reports from American missile bases. A retired US Army colonel named Karl Nell says records released under a US law that lets anyone request government files, along with witness accounts, back this up, which would mean the same thing happened on both sides of the Cold War.
soviet-paleocontact-theories: In the Soviet Union, Michels says, two figures named Alexander Kazantsev and Felix Zigel put forward the idea that alien visitors may have shaped early human development. He tells this himself, without naming where he read it. It matters to his story because it shows the idea of ancient alien contact was taken up on the Soviet side too, not only in the West.
soviet-phobos-probe-s-last-image-before-: In 1989 a Soviet probe sent to Phobos, one of the moons of Mars, stopped working, and its last image is said to show a strange object. Michels describes it himself, without naming a source: "an object like a fin on the tail of a plane." He raises it in an episode about claims that NASA hides unusual space data, as a hint that something was out there near Mars.
soviet-psychics-tasked-against-us-congre: The Soviet Union is said to have trained its psychics to spy on American congressmen, senators, cabinet members and the president. Joe McMoneagle, a man who worked as a psychic spy, tells it from a box of material about the Soviet psychic unit that he says he saw. If true, it would mean the Soviets aimed mind spying at the top of the US government.
soviet-psychokinesis-experiments-on-mice: In the 1970s, Soviet researchers are said to have taken mice down in submarines and tried to stop their hearts using psychokinesis, the supposed power of the mind to act directly on matter. The philosopher Jason Jorjani mentions it in passing, as proof that the same power could be used to kill a person.
soviet-spy-at-1950-pearl-harbor-demo-wou: In 1950, during a demonstration at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, the work of the inventor Townsend Brown was compromised by a Soviet spy posing as a janitor. Michels tells this in a documentary about Brown, drawing on The Man Who Mastered Gravity, a book by Brown's biographer Paul Schatzkin. It would mean the Soviets thought Brown's work worth spying on.
soviet-target-mice-psi-experiment-in-the: A Soviet psychic research unit in the Ural Mountains ran an experiment with mice, and the results came out perfectly: "top 12 and bottom 12, it was a perfect match, all the bottom ones were controls, all the top ones were target mice." A former US Army psychic spy named Joe McMoneagle says he read this in a box of material from the Soviet unit. If true, it would mean the Soviets got a clean result showing a mental effect on living animals.
soviet-ukraine-missiles-enter-countdown-: In 1982, a huge disc-shaped object is said to have hovered over a Soviet nuclear missile base in Ukraine, and down in one of the launch rooms the missiles suddenly went into countdown mode on their own. The researcher Robert Hastings, who studies UFO reports at nuclear weapons sites, tells it from classified Soviet UFO files obtained by the Las Vegas journalist George Knapp, and from a witness account involving a man named Vladimir Plantonoff. If true, it would mean these objects could interfere with nuclear weapons.
soviet-version-of-operation-paperclip-19: After the Second World War, the Soviet Union ran its own version of Operation Paperclip, the US program that brought German scientists to America, and took more than 3,000 scientists and their families into Russia. The author Peter Levenda tells this, drawing on a book called Secret Machines. It shows that the race for German know-how was not only an American one.
space-act-of-1958-ties-nasa-to-dod-and-a: The National Aeronautics and Space Act, the law Congress passed in 1958 to create NASA, is said to bind the space agency closely to the Department of Defense and let it keep certain findings secret. If that is so, anything sensitive NASA found could stay hidden. Maaneli Derakhshani, a guest on the podcast, makes the basic point, saying NASA and the Defense Department "have always been very tightly linked in law" through that act. Michels goes further in his own narration of a separate episode. He says findings judged "outside the civilian mandate" could be held back. In practice, he says, that meant a breakthrough in propulsion, a powerful new sensor, "or even contact with non-human intelligence" could be "withheld indefinitely." Both describe the law in their own words rather than quoting its text.
space-force-people-ask-about-hawkeye-360: In 2022, at a meeting of the Scientific Coalition for UAP Studies in Huntsville, Alabama (UAP, or unidentified anomalous phenomena, is the government's newer term for UFOs), people tied to the Space Force, the US military's space branch, and to intelligence agencies approached Bob Maguire about using the abilities of Hawkeye 360 to look for UAP signals on the ground. Maguire, a former CIA contractor, says this happened to him directly. If true, it would mean military people were quietly looking for ways to track such objects.
space-intelligences-chose-owens-for-the-: A man named Ted Owens claimed that intelligences from space picked him out because he had the most powerful nervous system of anyone they had met since Moses. The parapsychologist Jeffrey Mishlove, who knew Owens's claims, relays this as what Owens himself would say. If true, it would mean these beings chose their human contacts for something in their bodies and minds.
space-kid-channels-an-egyptian-god-insid: In 1976, inside the Great Pyramid at Giza in Egypt, the researcher Andrija Puharich reportedly ran experiments with one of the young people known as the "space kids," who then seemed to channel, or speak for, an Egyptian god. An unnamed researcher on the show tells it without a source, saying "they brought through this information." If true, messages would have come through a person from some outside intelligence.
space-kid-shows-copper-bracelet-worn-in-: A woman who took part as a child in 1970s channeling sessions, where messages were said to come from other beings through a person, still had the copper bracelet the children wore during them. She showed it decades later, says a researcher named Greg Malatzi, who saw it while filming an interview with her. He tells Michels that "she whipped out this bracelet," with a small copper plate on it, that "they all had to wear" in the sessions with the CIA scientist who ran them. The bracelet is real-world evidence that the sessions happened.
space-kids-channeling-tapes-name-israeli: On recordings made in the 1970s, a scientist named Andrija Puharich, whom the episode calls a CIA scientist, is heard naming Israeli generals such as Aharon Yariv. The tapes are of channeling sessions, where a person speaks messages said to come from another intelligence, held with a group of young people called the space kids, around Ossining, New York. A researcher named Greg Malatzi describes what is on the tapes in summary, as something that would tie the sessions to real military figures.
space-program-insiders-learn-their-missi: People inside the US space program, so the story goes, are never told what their missions are: they have to work them out alone. The religious studies scholar Diana Pasulka tells Michels she spent enough time around such people to see it, saying they "figured out their missions not from asking people," found it hard, and only learned they had guessed right when they received an award about two years later.
space-program-latin-symbols-as-homage-to: The mission patches made for American space launches are said to carry Latin symbols and Greek goddess imagery, and some people in that world reportedly say these are a tribute to beings they call "the sponsors." Diana Pasulka, a scholar of religion, tells this from what her sources told her: a man she calls Tyler, who worked on launches, saw imagery he did not understand, and when she asked whether the sponsors could read Latin, people answered "absolutely." In another telling she places it in today's Space Force, the US military branch for space, and talks only about the patches, without the tribute to the sponsors.
space-scientist-david-w-webb-and-governm: By the mid 1980s, when strange visits were happening at his cabin in upstate New York, the writer Whitley Strieber already knew that some people inside the government had had contact with beings. He says he learned this from meeting a space scientist named David W. Webb. Strieber tells it himself, as part of his own account of being visited, and as a sign that officials knew about such experiences.
spacecraft-momentum-anomalies-in-the-van: Spacecraft orbiting the Earth either speed up or slow down for no clear reason when they reach the Van Allen belts, zones of charged particles trapped around the planet. Charles Buhler, an engineer who has worked at NASA, the US space agency, mentions these momentum oddities without naming a source, as a sign that space may hold forces we do not yet understand.
spacecraft-recovered-from-aztec-kingman-: A spacecraft was recovered near Aztec, New Mexico, in the late 1940s, according to the Australian journalist Ross Coulthart, who says the former intelligence officer and whistleblower David Grusch told him so in passing. Michels tells a fuller version himself: on March 25, 1948, a flying saucer about 100 feet across crashed in the New Mexico desert with 16 charred alien bodies inside, and several eyewitnesses saw it from different spots. If true, it would mean a second crashed craft, and its crew, came into human hands soon after the better-known 1947 stories.
spaceship-reportedly-landed-and-was-hush: Barry Goldwater, a US senator, is heard saying that reportedly a spaceship had landed and that it was all hushed up and kept quiet. The story is tied to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, an Air Force base in Ohio, and if true would mean the government hid a landed craft.
special-forces-guys-play-hunter-skinwalk: Three armed former special forces men went onto Skinwalker Ranch, a Utah property known for reports of strange happenings, planning to play "Hunter Skinwalker" and hunt whatever was there. The UFO researcher Grant Cameron tells it as he heard it from Brandon Fugal, the ranch's owner, without saying how it turned out.
special-programs-bring-secret-technology: Secret government programs brought their own hidden technology to events run by Skywatcher, a startup that tries to call up UFOs, without telling the company, and people were then asked to sign nondisclosure agreements, contracts that bind them to secrecy. James Valor of Skywatcher says this from his own part in those projects at US military events in the 2020s, and if true it would mean some of what the group saw in the sky may have been secret human craft.
special-ufo-briefing-for-maintenance-tea: In 1967 at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, a base that held nuclear missiles, maintenance crews were called into a special briefing and told there were UFOs in the area. The former Air Force officer Robert Salas tells this as what a man named Robert Jameson, who was on those crews, told him. If true, it would mean the Air Force knew of the objects and warned its own men about them.
spectre-modeled-on-odessa-1945: SPECTRE, the made-up criminal organisation in the James Bond spy novels by the writer Ian Fleming, was really based on a group Fleming knew as ODESSA, a secret network that the claim ties to the end of the Second World War in 1945. Jason Jorjani, a researcher who says he has found a secret Nazi UFO programme, makes this case to Jesse Michels without naming a source, and he links the network to two figures from Hitler's circle, the aide Martin Bormann and the commando Otto Skorzeny. If he is right, the Bond books were hiding a real postwar Nazi network in plain sight.
speculation-that-kirkpatrick-was-read-in: Sean Kirkpatrick, the first head of the Pentagon office set up in 2022 to study unexplained aerial reports, was speculated to have been "read into" the legacy program, meaning he was given access to it. The legacy program is a long-running secret effort that some claim handles recovered non-human craft. Kurt McConnell, a former US Senate staffer, mentions the speculation in passing. If true, it would mean the man running the public inquiry knew about the secret effort.
sperm-sampling-and-insect-like-faces-197: In 1976, on the Allagash Waterway in Maine, a man named Jim Weiner says he was taken by beings who sampled his sperm and whose faces looked like insects. He tells Michels it as something that happened to him, and says their faces only came back to him in a second session of remembering: "I remember screaming, 'They're bugs. They look like bugs.'" If true, it would be a detailed case of beings taking people and collecting samples from them.
sphere-crash-south-of-the-border-that-ki: A sphere is said to have crashed about 100 miles south of the US border near Brownsville, Texas, on Mexico's east coast, and the explosion killed a cow 100 meters away. Steve Colbern, a scientist who studies objects said to be alien implants, tells it second-hand: a man named Massan bought the sphere from the farmer who owned the land and passed on the farmer's account. If true, it would be a recovered crashed object in private hands.
sphere-described-as-a-control-mechanism-: In 2014, at Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane in Indiana, a Navy research base, staff described a sphere as possibly "part of a control mechanism" that "interacted with conscious[ness]," meaning it responded to the mind. Randy Anderson, who says he saw alien technology at the base, tells Michels he remembers them saying this. If true, it would mean the military holds a device that is worked by thought.
sphere-holds-15-ft-from-a-friend-s-cockp: A fighter pilot flying near Patuxent River, a naval air station in Maryland, had a sphere pull up about 15 feet from his cockpit while he was maneuvering fast, and it stayed there beside him for a while. The former Navy fighter pilot Ryan Graves tells this as the case of one of his good friends, without naming him. If true, it would mean something could keep pace with a jet at arm's length.
sphere-inside-a-cube-near-miss-at-oceana: Around 2014 or 2015, off the coast of Virginia, a strange object shaped like a dark cube inside a clear sphere nearly hit a pair of Navy fighter jets, passing within about 50 feet of the lead plane's cockpit. A Navy fighter pilot named Ryan Graves tells it about fellow pilots in his squadron and says a hazard report, the Navy's formal safety report, was filed. Jesse Michels repeats Graves's account, and a retired Navy admiral named Tim Gallaudet, also citing Graves, places it during a carrier training exercise and says the object split the two jets apart.
sphere-leaves-in-eight-seconds-1976: In 1976, on Eagle Lake along the Allagash Waterway in Maine, a glowing sphere shot away and shrank to a pinpoint of light in the night sky in just eight seconds, says Charlie Foltz, who says he was there. He timed it from the moment he spotted it until it was a dot: "8 seconds had elapsed." He tells it as part of an episode about people who say they were abducted, and the speed is what struck him.
sphere-recovered-from-a-crashed-craft-20: At Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane, a Navy research base in Indiana, a sphere was shown in 2014 that the people there said had been recovered from a craft that had crashed. A man named Randy Anderson, who says he saw alien technology at a military base, tells Jesse Michels he was there and heard them say it, which, if true, would point to the military holding parts from crashed craft.
spheres-entering-the-water-at-guadalupe-: Around 2019, two men named Luis Elizondo and Sean Cahill went to Guadalupe Island, off Mexico, because there had been reports of spheres flying into the water there. A guest named Marik von Rennenkampff tells it, linking the trip to a National Geographic television series called Unidentified. If true, it would point to unknown objects that move between the air and the sea.
sphinx-enclosure-filled-in-and-excavated: The Sphinx in Egypt may be older than usually thought, because the pharaoh Thutmose IV recorded that its enclosure, the pit carved around it, was filled in and that he had to dig it all out and clean it before becoming pharaoh. A researcher named Luke Caverns makes this argument, saying this came about a thousand years after the Sphinx's accepted date, and that the usual account ignores it.
sphinx-enclosure-opening-said-to-connect: There are three openings at the back of the walled area around the Sphinx in Giza, Egypt, and one of them connects into the Queen's Chamber, a room inside the Great Pyramid. So says Geoffrey Drumm, a guest who offers his own theory of what the pyramids were for. He says an unnamed friend in Egypt's Ministry of Antiquities, the government office that runs its ancient sites, confirmed it to him. If so, it would mean hidden passages link the Sphinx and the pyramid.
sphinx-originally-had-a-lion-s-head: The Great Sphinx in Egypt, the tellers say, was first carved as a full lion, and its human head was cut later. The writer Graham Hancock makes this argument, building on the researchers Robert Schoch and John Anthony West, and says the pharaohs recarved the head. Michels repeats it, crediting Hancock, and adds that a lion would have matched the constellation Leo, which marked the spring equinox around 10,500 BC. A researcher named Matt LaCroix points to the head being too small for the body as the evidence that it was recarved by later Egyptians. If true, the Sphinx would be far older than usually thought.
sphinx-outcrop-was-always-visible-from-t: The researcher Luke Caverns argues that the Sphinx in Egypt was carved from a huge limestone outcrop that people living along the Nile must always have known was there. He gives this as his own reading, without naming a source. If he is right, the rock would have been a known landmark long before anyone carved it, which bears on how old the site really is.
spider-bite-leads-fox-to-one-of-the-girl: In 2012, in Varginha, Brazil, a spider bite led the filmmaker James Fox to someone close to one of the girls in the town's famous alien case, where an army is said to have caught a live creature. Fox tells Michels that a man he met because of the bite said, "Oh my gosh, I dated one of the girls." The chance meeting gave him a way to reach a witness.
spielberg-approached-by-naval-intelligen: After the film director Steven Spielberg made his shark film Jaws, he was supposedly approached by men from Naval Intelligence, the US Navy's intelligence service, who offered him a deal, and he took it. A man named Brent Friedman says he heard this around 1995, in Newhall, California, from the director Tobe Hooper, who told him Spielberg "got approached by some guys from naval intelligence or something." The story appears again in clips of the same telling, one of which credits Hooper but stops before saying whether Spielberg accepted. If true, it would mean the military had a hand in Spielberg's later films.
spielberg-based-the-close-encounters-sci: When the film director Steven Spielberg made Close Encounters of the Third Kind, his 1977 movie about contact with UFOs, he based the eccentric but brilliant UFO scientist, played by Francois Truffaut, on the UFO researcher Jacques Vallée. Michels tells this himself while introducing Vallée as his guest, as a measure of how influential Vallée has been.
spielberg-binge-watched-the-secret-of-sk: The film director Steven Spielberg is said to have binge-watched all 72 episodes of The Secret of Skinwalker Ranch, a TV series about a Utah property famous for strange sightings, before making his film Disclosure Day, pointing to the congressional hearings and the government's growing acknowledgement that the phenomenon is real. Brandon Fugal, the businessman who owns the ranch, relays this as Spielberg told it, which suggests that one of the world's best-known filmmakers took the show seriously.
spielberg-s-ea-game-lmno-about-a-woman-w: Around 2004, the film director Steven Spielberg worked on a video game for the game company Electronic Arts, code-named LMNO, about a human woman with alien abilities who uses the power of empathy to disarm people while the government hunts her. Brent Friedman, a writer who says he was involved, tells Michels this himself, as part of a wider story about Hollywood, the CIA and UFOs.
spielberg-s-letter-to-james-fox-about-i-: Steven Spielberg, the film director, sent a letter to James Fox, a maker of UFO documentaries, about Fox's 2009 film I Know What I Saw. Jesse Michels tells it himself, saying Fox revealed the letter, but he gives nothing of what it said. He brings it up as a sign that Spielberg paid attention to serious UFO work.
spielberg-s-live-imax-interview-for-disc: In 2026, the film director Steven Spielberg spoke in a live interview at an IMAX theater tied to Disclosure Day, his UFO film, and said something there that Bryce Zabel brings up. Zabel, a guest on an episode about Hollywood, the Central Intelligence Agency and UFOs, says he and Michels watched the interview together "last night." The telling does not say in these words what Spielberg said.
spielberg-s-tip-about-the-ariel-school-l: The film director Steven Spielberg reportedly passed on a tip that the Ariel School landing was worth looking into. That is a 1990s case at a school in Ruwa, Zimbabwe, where a craft is said to have landed near the children. James Fox, a documentary filmmaker who investigates UFOs, tells it from what he was told, naming Spielberg and the film producer Janet Yang as the people the tip came through. It is part of how he came to investigate the case.
spielberg-tells-robert-liefeld-ufos-may-: The film director Steven Spielberg is said to have asked comic book artist Robert Liefeld, the creator of the character Deadpool, in 1993 what was easier to believe: that aliens from another world are watching us, or that we are studying ourselves from the future. Jesse Michels repeats this several times, citing Liefeld, and tells it a little differently each time, once naming far-off star systems as the alternative and once saying flatly that Spielberg told Liefeld the aliens were time travelers. If it reflects Spielberg's real view, one of the best-known UFO filmmakers privately leaned toward the idea that the visitors are future humans.
spielberg-ufos-as-future-humans-2020: The film director Steven Spielberg has wondered aloud whether UFOs come not from a civilisation hundreds of millions of light years away but from us, humans 500,000 years in the future. The remark, made to the talk-show host Stephen Colbert, comes up in an episode with the hip-hop artist Flying Lotus. If true, it would mean the visitors are our own descendants.
spillage-reported-up-the-chain-told-to-g: In 2018, a Pentagon whistleblower named Matthew Brown says he came across secret material about unexplained objects sitting where it did not belong, which insiders call a "spillage". He reported it to a superior in the Pentagon office that oversees its most secret programs, and he says the man "basically recommended to me, delete that and pretend he never saw it, and then he just left the room." Brown tells this from his own experience and ties it to a document he calls the Immaculate Constellation capabilities briefing. If true, it would mean officials were quietly burying such reports rather than passing them on.
spinning-mercury-in-the-vimanas: The vimanas, flying machines described in old Indian texts, are said to have run on spinning mercury. Michels mentions it himself in passing, without a source. Kurt McConnell, a former US Senate staffer, describes them as rotating cylinders filled with a form of mercury, also without naming a source. He points out that this is the same thing Igor Witkowski, a writer on secret Nazi weapons, says was being done in the Bell, a device said to have been built in a Nazi programme. If true, it would tie an ancient Indian idea to a modern secret propulsion project.
spiritualism-wave-seances-as-common-as-c: In the 1800s and early 1900s, a craze for spiritualism, the belief that the living can talk with the dead, swept America and Europe, and at its height going to a seance, a gathering to contact spirits, was said to be as common on a Sunday morning as going to church. The filmmaker Tim Alberino tells it from newspaper and magazine articles of that time he came across while working on a project called Birthright, without naming them. He tells it to show how widespread contact with unseen beings once seemed to ordinary people.
spock-s-reverence-for-the-sun-1990: Sometime between 1990 and 1993, at the first overseas base of a secret programme he says he served in, a contact Dan Sherman calls Spock spoke to him about the sun, saying that people "really don't understand the value" of it. Sherman, a former Air Force sergeant who says the National Security Agency, the US spy agency that intercepts communications, hired him to talk with aliens, tells this as something he lived through. He also tells it in his book Above Black, and if true it would mean an otherworldly voice was teaching him a way of seeing the cosmos.
spock-says-you-can-go-around-time-1990: Between 1990 and 1993, at his first overseas posting, a being he calls Spock told him that "you can go around time". The story comes from Dan Sherman, a former Air Force sergeant who says the National Security Agency hired him to communicate with aliens. He tells it as his own experience, and admits he did not really understand what was meant.
sport-model-came-from-an-underwater-arch: The disc-shaped craft nicknamed the "sport model", which Bob Lazar says he worked on in 1989 at S4, a secret site near the Nevada base known as Area 51, came from an archaeological dig that was not in the desert but under water. Lazar says a man named Barry Castilio told him this, and Michels later repeats it, saying Lazar has recently reworded his old "archaeological dig" into "a Navy find on the seafloor", while the researcher Tim Alberino recalls only that the craft were ancient and another telling says just one of the craft came from the sea floor. If true, it would mean at least one recovered craft was pulled from the ocean by the Navy, not found in a crash on land.
spotting-the-nsa-by-where-number-theory-: You could find the National Security Agency, the secret US agency that makes and breaks codes, by checking where people with doctorates in number theory (the maths of whole numbers, which codes rely on) live when they don't take a visible university job: they cluster around Fort Meade, Maryland. The mathematician Eric Weinstein offers this to Michels as his own reasoning, without naming a source. The point is that secret work leaves traces in where its experts quietly settle.
squadron-safety-survey-turns-up-four-mor: After a near collision with an unknown object, a Navy fighter pilot named Ryan Graves says his squadron near Virginia Beach filed a hazard report, the military's formal safety report, and a follow-up survey found "like four other near midairs" with the same issue over the past few months that had never been reported. Graves tells Michels this as someone who was in the squadron at the time. He tells it to show that pilots were having close calls with these objects and keeping quiet about them.
squanto-unites-three-rival-tribes: A Native American man named Squanto, in what is now Massachusetts, is said to have brought together three tribes that had been rivals and formed them into a single federation. A researcher named Luke Caverns tells this on an episode with Michels about the pyramids, offering it as an example of one figure uniting peoples who had been at odds.
squared-off-object-tumbles-into-the-back: In the 1950s, at his family's country house in Texas, the writer Whitley Strieber says, a square-edged object came tumbling across the sky and fell into the field behind the house. Strieber tells Michels it as something from his own childhood, "this object that was squared off came tumbling across the sky and went into the back pasture," and he mentions a man named Karl Strieber in the story. If true, it would be an early brush with a crashed craft in his family's life.
sr-71-pilot-encourages-sherman-to-join-t: A pilot of the SR-71, a very fast, high-flying American spy plane, strongly urged a young Dan Sherman to join the Air Force. Sherman tells this from his own life. He is a former Air Force sergeant who says the National Security Agency, the US government's code-breaking and eavesdropping agency, later hired him to communicate with aliens, and he points to his book Above Black for his story.
sri-and-at-t-chairman-meeting-on-unackno: In the 1990s, a chairman of SRI, a research institute, and of AT&T, the telephone company, met to discuss unacknowledged projects, secret programmes whose existence the government does not admit. Steven Greer, a campaigner for UFO disclosure, tells Michels he was at the meeting himself. He tells it to suggest that big private companies help hold UFO secrets.
sri-pay-stub-to-puharich-s-lab-nine-1973: A 1973 pay stub from SRI, a research institute in California, to Lab Nine, the private lab of the researcher Andrija Puharich in Ossining, New York, is said to sit in Puharich's archives. Greg Malatzi, a researcher who has gone through those archives, uses it to dismiss the claim that something "disappeared" with a flat "Not true," and he ties it to Hal Puthoff, a physicist at SRI. If genuine, the stub would show that money moved from SRI to Puharich's lab that year.
sri-psi-research-1960: Michels mentions that in the late 1960s and early 1970s, SRI, a research institute in California, carried out research into psychic abilities. He brings it up in passing, without details or a source, during a talk about UFOs, coincidences and dreams that seem to foretell the future. He offers it as an example of serious researchers taking the mind's stranger powers seriously.
ss-officers-freemasons-and-occultists-ru: By the mid-1960s, Michels says, the real power structure of NASA, the US space agency, was "a strange cocktail of former SS officers, Freemasons, and occultists." The SS was the elite force of Nazi Germany, the Freemasons are a centuries-old secret fraternal society, and occultists practise hidden or magical traditions. Michels tells this himself, without naming a single source, in an episode on what he sees as the hidden ritual and secret side of the space program.
ss-tibet-expedition-of-1938: In 1938 the SS, the Nazi party's elite force, sent an expedition to Tibet. It is brought up as a sign of the Nazi leadership's interest in ancient and hidden knowledge. The author Peter Levenda says he studied it in captured German documents on microfilm, and he ties it to Heinrich Himmler, the head of the SS. The philosopher Jason Jorjani mentions it in an episode about what he calls Hitler's secret UFO programme. He gives no year but says the Nazis "even sent people to Tibet" to obtain Tibetan scriptures. He also brings in Mount Kailash, a sacred mountain in Tibet. Levenda speaks from the files and Jorjani from his own research, without a named source.
ssris-that-made-him-suicidal-his-psychia: Around 2016 and 2017, doctors at the VA, the US government health service for military veterans, put a man named Dylan Borland on antidepressants called SSRIs, and he says they made him suicidal. He tells it himself, pointing to his VA medical records, and says that is the reason his first doctor quit his case.
st-andrews-study-finds-magnetic-signatur: A study by the University of St Andrews in Scotland looked under the ground at the Callanish stone circle, an ancient ring of standing stones, and found a magnetic signature left by lightning striking there again and again. Geoffrey Drumm, a guest who studies ancient sites like the pyramids, summarises the paper himself, as a sign that such old stone sites may have been tied to electricity.
st-francis-of-assisi-s-stigmata-as-ufo-r: Saint Francis of Assisi, praying on Mount La Verna in Italy in the 1200s, saw something come out of the sky with sparks, a spinning disk and a flaming torch, and the wounds he got on his hands, the stigmata, were really radiation or electromagnetic burns from that encounter, according to the host. Michels tells it again and again across many episodes, crediting the religion scholar Diana Pasulka and her book American Cosmic, and he says the earliest accounts, by Francis's companion Brother Leo and by the early biographer Thomas of Celano, speak of sparks and a torch rather than Christ; once he adds that Francis died of the effects a year later. Pasulka herself, telling it from the original sources, says Leo, about 15, watched the thing deal harshly with Francis and leave him injured, but she does not call it radiation.
st-francis-s-final-tau: The medieval saint Francis of Assisi is said to have seen a seraph, a fiery angel, which Michels suggests was probably a craft or an orb, and the last thing he wrote in his diary was the Greek letter Tau, which Michels says means conversion. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, in a conversation about angels and UFOs in the Bible, as an example of an old religious vision that might describe the same thing people now call UFOs.
st-mary-s-chapel-at-glastonbury-abbey-ke: St Mary's Chapel at Glastonbury Abbey, an old abbey in England, is 39.6 feet wide, and that width is said to preserve the diameter of the first chapel built on the spot. The researcher Randall Carlson passes this on as something that is said, without naming a source, as a sign that an older sacred measure was kept alive in the later building.
st-patrick-s-day-argument-darpa-as-corso: A DARPA scientist named John Blitch says that during a St Patrick's Day argument in a DARPA office, he built the case that DARPA, the Pentagon's agency for advanced research, grew out of the Army section where Philip J. Corso worked under a General Trudeau. Corso is the man behind the book The Day After Roswell, which Blitch draws on, and Roswell refers to the 1947 crash in New Mexico said by some to involve a craft not from Earth. In Blitch's argument, DARPA became "the conduit to break up all the component Technologies and distribute them", which would mean crash material was quietly fed into American research.
stack-five-ceremonial-magic-program-at-w: There was once a program at Wright Field, a US military airfield, called Stack Five, or "ST5," that carried out "bizarre magical protocols, ceremonial magic." Michels says this himself, as something he believes, without naming a source or a date. If true, it would mean the military had dabbled in the occult.
staff-found-the-kalmykian-president-miss: The president of Kalmykia, a small republic inside Russia, is said to have vanished from a locked room for about an hour and then reappeared. He has called this being taken by aliens. The president, Kiran Ilum Xenov, tells it himself. He places it in a Moscow apartment in September 1997. He says his friends "were already in the apartment looking for me for over an hour and couldn't find me." A witness named Vasili, who says he was there, dates it to September 17, 1997. He says that after maybe an hour "he appears from the bedroom, even though he wasn't there before." Michels tells it a little differently. He says he has the president's staff on record saying they went into his room, "his clothes were missing, and we couldn't find him anywhere." He also cites the chess champion Garry Kasparov. If true, it would mean a sitting head of a region physically disappeared during a contact experience.
stan-marcus-tells-nick-cook-the-bell-slo: During the 1940s, the Germans were able to slow time inside the field around a device called the bell, a machine Nazi Germany is said to have built. A man named Stan Marcus told this to his contact Nick Cook, who describes the field as a torsion field, a kind of twisting energy field. Michels repeats the claim as Cook's source gave it, and if it were true, it would mean the bell could change time itself.
stan-meyer-collection-group-killed: All but one of the men who got hold of the papers and devices left by the inventor Stan Meyer, including a ring-shaped device called a toroid, are said to have been killed. Steven Greer, a doctor who campaigns for UFO disclosure, tells it from what he was told, and he names an unnamed British lord as one source. The story touches Michigan, the United Kingdom and Orange County, California. Greer tells it as a sign that people are killed over energy technology.
stan-meyer-poisoned-per-his-twin-steve-1: An inventor named Stan Meyer, who died in 1998, was poisoned and killed, according to his twin brother Steve Meyer, who is said to be fully convinced of it. Steven Greer, a campaigner who says a global group keeps UFO secrets, passes this on as what the brother believes. Greer tells it as an example of inventors being silenced.
stan-meyer-water-dissociation-and-zero-p: An inventor named Stan Meyer found that at certain frequencies water would split into hydrogen and oxygen using less electricity than standard chemistry, set by a value called the Faraday constant, says is needed. Steven Greer, a campaigner for UFO disclosure, tells this and ties it to zero point energy, the idea of drawing power from empty space, crediting a book called The Lost Century. If true, it would mean cheap fuel from water had been found.
stan-romanek-contactee-and-hybrid-photog: In the 2000s, north of Denver, Colorado, a man named Stan Romanek said he was in regular contact with beings, and his wife is said to have photographed one of the part-human, part-alien "hybrids." The UFO researcher Grant Cameron tells it, calling Romanek "a major contactee," someone who says he has ongoing contact with beings, who "had all these beings" around him. Cameron tells it as a case he knew of, with the photograph as its evidence.
stanford-team-finds-two-cavities-under-k: In the 1970s a team from Stanford University scanned the Khafre pyramid, the second of the great pyramids at Giza in Egypt, and confirmed an earlier finding of two hidden cavities underneath it. A researcher named Luke Caverns tells this, without naming his source. If so, there are spaces beneath the pyramid that have never been explained.
stanley-mcdaniel-s-book-on-nasa-s-failur: In the 1990s, a professor emeritus at Sonoma State University named Stanley McDaniel wrote a 200-page book arguing that NASA, the US space agency, failed to properly investigate what he saw as structures on the surface of Mars. Michels brings up the book himself, on an episode with a guest named Joe McMoneagle about life on Mars. If McDaniel was right, the agency would have looked away from possible signs of something built on another planet.
starfish-prime-bluegill-triple-prime-emp: In 1962 the United States set off nuclear bombs high above the Pacific in a test series called Starfish Prime, and in doing so accidentally created an EMP, an electromagnetic pulse, a burst of energy that can knock out electronics. Michels says this himself during a debate with a skeptic, naming one of those tests, Bluegill Triple Prime, as coming four years before the events he was discussing. He raises it to tie nuclear testing to what came after.
stargate-as-a-vestibule-for-a-deeper-bla: Stargate, a US government program run partly at a California research institute that studied whether people could see distant places with their minds, was shut down in 1995, but Michels suggests it was only a "vestibule" for a deeper, fully secret project that still exists. He says a remote-viewing subject named Pat Price was recruited into that hidden project and was killed over it. Michels says this himself, without naming a source, in a conversation with a philosopher.
stargate-ends-in-1995-and-puharich-is-si: Stargate, a US government programme that used psychics to try to see distant places with the mind, officially ended in 1995, and the government then filled the news with articles saying there was nothing to it and it was all bunk. An unnamed researcher tells this to Jesse Michels, drawing on the journalist Annie Jacobsen and tying it to Andrija Puharich, a researcher of psychic abilities who, the story says, was silenced. The point of telling it is that the public dismissal may have been a cover rather than an honest ending.
stargate-files-declassified-2017: Stargate, a US government programme that used psychics as spies, was declassified in 2017, and all its files are now online, according to Michels. He tells this himself, without naming a source, to point out that anyone can read the records of the programme for themselves.
stargate-inscriptions-at-dendera: Inscriptions at Dendera, an ancient temple site in Egypt, are said to translate literally as "stargate." Michels tells it twice. The first time he credits Ben van Kerkwijk, a researcher of ancient sites, who talked about it on another podcast. The second time he gives no source and says the hieroglyphs are below Dendera. If true, it would hint that the ancient Egyptians wrote about some kind of gateway to the stars.
stargate-psychic-spy-program-1972-1995: From 1972 to 1995, the US government is said to have paid people to spy with their minds in a programme called Stargate. It used "remote viewing", the attempt to describe distant or hidden places by mental focus alone. Jesse Michels returns to it often and says it was backed first by the CIA and later by the Defense Intelligence Agency, the military's spy service. He says its targets included Russian nuclear bases and American hostages, and that its files were released in 2017 under FOIA, a US law that lets anyone request government records. The physicist Hal Puthoff, who helped found it with Russell Targ, tells it from the inside: it began with viewing secret facilities and project names locked in safes and grew into "a 20-year 20 million dollar program". Joe McMoneagle, who took part as a viewer, says it had the support of five presidents and senators such as John Glenn, and that it ended because of stigma, not because it failed. Michels notes that many said afterward it was not very effective, and that the official reason for closing it was that it offered "only offense" and no defence. Others back it up in their own ways: the whistleblower David Grusch passes on what Puthoff told him about viewers' reports being confirmed by normal intelligence, the former Pentagon official Luis Elizondo calls Puthoff the programme's "Godfather", and a former official named Matthew Brown talks about the trouble of putting psychics on the payroll. If it worked as they say, governments really did use the mind as a spying tool.
stargate-psychic-spy-program-made-public: Stargate was a US government program that tried to use psychics to spy, and Michels says it was eventually wrested from the government and made public around 2017. He tells this himself, without naming a source, while talking with the religion scholar Diana Pasulka. He brings it up as an example of secret government work on the unexplained coming into public view.
stargate-recruitment-6-of-600-people-tes: When the US government ran Stargate, its secret programme of "remote viewers", people said to be able to see distant places with the mind, it reached out to about 600 people, and only six turned out to have real talent. All six are said to have had synesthesia, a condition where the senses blend together. The magician and video maker Chris Ramsay tells this to Michels without naming a source.
stargate-staff-came-from-sidney-gottlieb: Many of the first people on Stargate, a US government program run from the 1970s to the 1990s at the Stanford Research Institute in California to study remote viewing (trying to describe distant places with the mind alone), are said to have come from a government technical services staff run by a man named Sidney Gottlieb. Michels says this himself, without naming a source, on an episode with a philosopher named Jason Jorjani. If true, it would tie the psychic program to an older and more secretive line of government work.
stargate-within-the-mesa: There may be a stargate, a kind of doorway to somewhere else, inside the mesa at Skinwalker Ranch, a Utah property known for reports of strange happenings. The ranch's owner floats this himself on Michels's show, framing it as an idea to imagine rather than something he has seen, and it would explain why so much odd activity centres on that rock.
staring-app-citizen-science-project-2024: In 2024 a phone app was being released so that ordinary people could test, and train, their sense of being stared at. The scientist Rupert Sheldrake describes it as his own project on Jesse Michels's show, saying it is an app "where you can train yourself to get better at it." If it worked, it would suggest that people can feel someone's gaze without seeing it.
starlink-trains-seen-from-shurmer-s-hous: From his home in the dark mountains above Santa Barbara, California, the researcher Michael Shermer says he regularly sees rocket launches and strings of Starlink satellites (small internet satellites that travel in a line, sometimes called trains) in the 2020s. He tells Michels this firsthand: Vandenberg, a military launch base about 90 miles up the coast, sends up a rocket about every week, and the sound reaches his house about six minutes later. He tells it to show that strange lights in the sky can have ordinary, human-made causes.
state-inspection-blocked-for-five-months: For five months in 2010, a children's services organisation called Baker Victory Services, in Springville, New York, is said to have refused to let state officials come in and inspect a boy in its care, before he was hastily sent home. That boy was Jordan Jose, who says he was taken into a secret UFO programme as a child, and he tells this to Jesse Michels from his own life. He says the record shows the five-month refusal, and he mentions the journalist Ross Coulthart in telling it. If true, it would mean someone was keeping him out of the authorities' sight.
station-wagon-woman-reappears-at-changi-: In 1990, a woman linked to an earlier encounter involving a station wagon turned up again at Changi Airport in Singapore. Peter Levenda, a writer described on the show as a historian of the CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, tells Jesse Michels he was at the airport himself when it happened, though in the words given he says little more than where he was. He offers it as a strange reappearance of the kind that suggests something guiding events.
stationary-objects-over-montana-written-: Objects were seen hanging almost still in the sky over Montana, and at the time people guessed they were Soviet spy planes. The UFO researcher Robert Hastings tells it. He says a controller told him the objects were "basically stationary," and he scoffs at the explanation: "are the Soviets flying helicopters over Montana? I don't think so." He tells it to suggest the objects were something other than ordinary aircraft.
stealth-bomber-over-altadena-on-new-year: The researcher Michael Shermer says he once saw a stealth bomber, a secretive US military plane with an unusual shape, fly over his house on New Year's Day when he lived in Altadena, California. He tells it firsthand as one of the examples he uses of an odd sight in the sky that turns out to have an ordinary explanation.
stealth-fighter-panels-rumored-to-be-ant: People would come to a US Air Force stealth fighter, pull panels out of it, put them in briefcases and leave, and the rumor was that some of those panels were anti-gravity devices that helped the plane fly in an unusual way. The author Greg Bishop passes this on from a man who told it to him. If true, it would mean anti-gravity technology was hidden inside a known military aircraft.
stefan-hogeborn-s-2012-dive-dark-black-s: In 2012 a diver named Stefan Hogeborn went down to an odd object on the floor of the Baltic Sea, brushed the sediment off it in near-freezing water, and found the surface underneath was dark black. The treasure hunter Dennis Asberg, whose team found the object and thinks it may be a UFO, tells this as what his diver saw. If true, it would be a first look at what the object is made of.
steinman-fired-by-lockheed-after-his-boo: A man named Bill Steinman was fired by Lockheed, a large American aircraft company, a couple of days after his book on flying saucers came out. According to Scott Ramsey, a researcher who studies a reported crash of alien craft, Steinman had been warned beforehand that the company did not like its employees writing books on flying saucers. Ramsey repeats what Steinman told him, and tells it as a sign of how unwelcome the subject was.
steinman-s-ufo-crash-book-aztec-1948-eri: A UFO researcher named William Steinman, in his book UFO Crash at Aztec, about a craft said to have come down near Aztec, New Mexico, in 1948, traced a head of special projects at Wright-Patterson, an Air Force base, named Eric Henry Wang, who had come to America through Operation Paperclip, the postwar programme that brought German scientists over, and Steinman concluded that Wang reported to someone called "HAK", meaning the future diplomat Henry Kissinger. Michels tells this himself across several episodes as something he has read, sometimes adding that Wang's wife, Maria Wang, said her husband worked on UFOs and his boss was Kissinger, and that when Steinman knocked on Wang's door "everything goes dark." If true, it would tie one of the most powerful men in American politics to the handling of crashed craft.
step-pyramid-as-methane-fracking-system: The Step Pyramid at Saqqara in Egypt was built as a system for fracking methane, meaning forcing water into rock under pressure to release gas. Geoffrey Drumm, who says an alien told him the true purpose of the pyramids, explains that an outside reservoir was used to raise and lower the water inside the pyramid "to increase and decrease pressure within your fracking tunnels." He names no source beyond his own reading of the site.
step-pyramid-design-at-angkor-thom: The same stepped pyramid shape found at ancient sites elsewhere also shows up at Angkor Thom, an ancient temple city in Cambodia. The researcher Matt LaCroix says he has seen it there himself, and mentions it in passing as one more place where the design repeats across distant cultures.
stephen-braude-s-first-person-plural-on-: The philosopher Stephen Braude of the University of Maryland, Baltimore, is said to have written in his first book, First Person Plural, about cases of multiple personality disorder that looked like possession. In that condition a person seems to hold several separate selves. The philosopher Jason Jorjani mentions the book and its chapter on these cases, as support for the idea that some outside mind might take hold of a person.
stephen-dick-paper-on-ufos-as-cellular-a: Steven J. Dick, an adviser to NASA, the US space agency, wrote a paper suggesting UFOs might be part of some kind of computational system, a bit like cellular automata, which are grids of cells following simple rules that build up complex patterns, according to Michels. Michels brings it up from memory and does not name the paper or say when it was written. If the idea holds, UFOs would be less like visiting ships and more like parts of a larger system steering events.
stephen-dick-s-early-suggestion-that-the: More than twenty years ago, the science historian Steven J. Dick suggested that the beings behind UFO sightings might be a form of artificial intelligence, or that if we ever met them, they would turn out to be one. Diana Pasulka, a professor who studies religion and UFO belief, credits him with the idea, mentioning him alongside the UFO researcher Jacques Vallée, to show the AI explanation is older than it seems.
stephen-hawking-s-submarine-trip-to-poss: The physicist Stephen Hawking once went down in a submarine to look at underwater ruins that some think could be the lost city of Atlantis, according to the comedian Kurt Metzger. He passes it on from a person he names as Fog Daniel and points to National Geographic, saying simply that Hawking 'went in a submarine to go look at that'.
stephen-miller-s-ufo-task-force-2026: In 2026, Stephen Miller, a longtime aide to President Donald Trump, is said to have put together a task force at the White House looking into UFOs. A congressman named Eric Burlison mentions it in passing, referring to "this task force that Stephen Miller has put together." Michels, in a later episode, describes Miller as the head of the Homeland Security Council and one of Trump's most loyal aides, and says Miller "owns the kind of UFO file for the White House" and that they are officially looking into it. The two differ in that Michels speaks of Miller holding the file rather than leading a task force. If true, the subject would now sit at the top of the US government.
sterilizing-world-physics-so-others-can-: The United States may have deliberately pushed people out of its physics and science programs so that the rest of the world could not catch up to what it had already achieved, according to the mathematician Eric Weinstein. He offers it as "one possibility", without a source. If true, it would mean physics was held back on purpose to protect a hidden lead.
steve-justice-at-to-the-stars-wanted-to-: Around 2017 to 2019, a man named Steve Justice, at To the Stars Academy, a private company set up to research UFOs, said he did not know how flying saucers flew and badly wanted to find out: "I want to know how they do it." The author Peter Levenda, who writes on the CIA and secret history, says Justice told him this himself. Levenda finds it striking because he saw Justice as someone who "would know where the bodies are buried", so his not knowing suggests even insiders lack the answer.
steven-dick-s-ai-protective-layer-of-ear: Earth may be wrapped in some kind of artificial intelligence that acts as a protective layer, according to an idea Michels credits to a former NASA figure named Steven Dick. Michels says Dick is part of the Galileo Project, an effort led by the Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb to look for signs of alien technology. Michels passes this along himself, hedging with "I think", as something he recalls Dick saying.
steven-greenstreet-s-one-night-visit-201: A reporter named Steven Greenstreet spent just one night at Skinwalker Ranch, a Utah property famous for reports of strange happenings, and arrived already sure of what he would find. That is the account of Brandon Fugal, the ranch's owner, who says Greenstreet "came in obviously with confirmation bias." Fugal raises it to argue that Greenstreet's doubts about the ranch are not worth much.
steven-greer-cut-the-four-fingered-arm-f: In a 2000 interview a witness named Jonathan Weygandt described a four-fingered arm, and Steven Greer, a campaigner for UFO disclosure, cut that part out of the footage, according to a researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb. He points to the raw files of the interview in Greer's archive, and names the filmmaker James Fox as part of the story. If true, it would mean an alien body detail was left out of what the public saw.
steven-greer-laurence-rockefeller-defect: Laurance Rockefeller, a member of the wealthy Rockefeller family, was a kind of defector from his own family in the 1990s, according to Steven Greer, a campaigner who pushes for the government to reveal what it knows about UFOs. Michels passes this on second hand as Greer's claim, suggesting Rockefeller broke ranks with his family on this subject.
steven-greer-s-benevolent-alien-theory: The UFO advocate Steven Greer holds that the beings behind UFOs are "all love and light and good," meaning friendly visitors with no ill intent. Michels sums up Greer's view this way during a debate with a skeptic, and he does not point to any particular work by Greer.
steven-greer-s-practice-of-calling-ufos-: A UFO researcher named Steven Greer is said to believe that ordinary people can call UFOs in on purpose, using a set of steps Michels calls the C5 protocols. Michels tells this himself on two episodes: in one he calls Greer a mixed bag but says his investigative work is now being vindicated, and in the other, speaking to a guest who had worked with Greer, he places the practice in the 1990s and adds that two men named Albert Stubblebine and John B. Alexander took an interest in it. If it worked, contact would not be something only governments could control.
steven-lovekin-eisenhower-doodled-ufos-a: In the 1950s, President Dwight D. Eisenhower is said to have doodled UFO drawings while inside Mount Weather, a government emergency bunker in Virginia, which was said to be where the UFO effort was headquartered. The UFO researcher Grant Cameron tells this second-hand from Stephen Lovekin, a man who says he was inside Mount Weather with Eisenhower, and he links the account to Steven Greer, a doctor who campaigns for UFO disclosure. If true, it would mean the president was personally close to the UFO matter.
steven-lovkin-eisenhower-said-he-no-long: Around 1959 or 1960, President Dwight D. Eisenhower is said to have doodled pictures of alien craft at the White House and, when asked about the subject, said "I don't have control of this anymore." Steven Greer tells this from the testimony of Stephen Lovekin, a young Army man in the signal corps, its communications branch, who worked at the White House and whose account Greer says is in his group's material. If true, it would mean even a president had lost control of the UFO issue.
stigmata-man-at-a-ufo-conference: A former Air Force sergeant named Dan Sherman, who says the National Security Agency (the US government's electronic spying agency) once hired him to communicate with aliens, recalls meeting a man at a UFO conference who had the stigmata. Stigmata are wounds on the body like the wounds of the crucified Christ. Sherman says he saw this himself, as part of describing the unusual people he met at such gatherings.
stigmatization-campaign-since-the-robert: The stigma around UFOs is said to be an eighty-year campaign, "very effective and well funded," that began with the Robertson Panel, a group of scientists the CIA convened in January 1953. A retired Navy admiral named Tim Gallaudet tells Michels this, which would mean public ridicule of the subject was planned. The panel's report, dated 16 February 1953, does call for a "debunking" aim to reduce public interest in "flying saucers" through "television, motion pictures, and popular articles," and urges agencies to "strip the Unidentified Flying Objects of the special status they have been given and the aura of mystery they have unfortunately acquired."
stonehenge-altar-stone-as-a-lightning-ro: Geoffrey Drumm, a researcher of ancient sites, claims the Altar Stone at Stonehenge, the large stone at the centre of the ancient circle in England, worked as a lightning rod, much like an obelisk. He tells it to Michels as his own view, without naming a source. If true, it would mean the monument was built as a kind of machine rather than only as a temple.
stones-floated-in-on-reed-boats-and-the-: The stones of the Egyptian pyramids at Giza were cut up the Nile, loaded onto reed boats and floated down, and the building site was flooded to bring them in. That is the account of Joe McMoneagle, a remote viewer, meaning someone who says he can see distant places and times with his mind, and he ties it to his book The Ultimate Time Machine. He gives it as his own finding, with no other source, and it would answer how the huge blocks were moved.
strange-deaths-of-abduction-researchers-: Several people who studied alien abductions are said to have died in strange ways, including John Mack, an abduction researcher, and another man also named John Mack, who were both supposedly hit by cars on the same day in England. The researcher Tim Alberino tells it from memory without a source ("if I recall"), and also names the abduction researchers Karla Turner, Budd Hopkins and Barbara Bartholic. He tells it to hint that the deaths might not be chance.
strange-explosions-caught-on-home-camera: Around 2022, strange explosions were picked up by the cameras at the home of Whitley Strieber, an author who says he has met non-human beings. Strieber tells this himself, saying the beings "got pissed off at me" and the explosions followed. To him, it is a sign that these visitors act on the physical world and react to what he does.
strange-lights-over-the-san-juan-coal-mi: A local man from Aztec, New Mexico, named Brett Lanner says he has seen strange lights darting above the San Juan coal mine, right by where he worked. Michels reports this from his own conversation with Lanner, as part of his reporting on a UFO crash said to have happened near Aztec. It hints that the area still sees odd activity today.
stranger-in-long-john-silver-s-says-read: In 1976, in a Long John Silver's fast-food restaurant near Fort Knox, the Army post in Kentucky, a stranger walked straight up to a young Rolf Mowatt-Larssen, told him "Read Ezekiel, Daniel, Revelations," three books of the Bible full of visions and prophecy, and walked away. Mowatt-Larssen, a former senior CIA officer, tells it as his own experience and describes the man in his book A State of Mind: Faith in the CIA. He tells it as an odd, pointed message that seemed meant for him.
stranger-with-air-force-ties-at-hart-can: In 2026, a stranger with curious ties to the US Air Force turned up at Hart Canyon, near Aztec, New Mexico, a remote, hard-to-reach spot, at the very moment Michels and his crew arrived. Michels tells this himself, as something that happened to him while looking into a reported crash there said to have left sixteen alien bodies, and the timing struck him as more than chance.
strassman-s-repeat-dose-dmt-tests-showin: In studies in the 1990s, the researcher Rick Strassman injected people with DMT, a powerful psychedelic drug, over and over, and found their bodies did not build up a tolerance to it. The neuroscientist Andrew Gallimore describes these tests without naming a source. If true, it would mean the brain treats DMT unlike most drugs, never getting used to it.
strassman-s-spirit-molecule-hypothesis-d: The idea that DMT, a strong psychedelic the body makes itself, is released at the moment of death, which is how it got the name the spirit molecule, comes from the psychiatrist Rick Strassman and his book DMT: The Spirit Molecule. The neuroscientist Andrew Gallimore explains where this common idea came from. If true, it would tie what people see near death to a chemical in the brain.
strategic-air-command-letter-congratulat: In the late 1970s, according to the author Peter Levenda, Strategic Air Command, the part of the US Air Force that ran the nuclear bombers and missiles, sent a friendly letter on its own letterhead congratulating the publishers of the Necronomicon, a book of supposed ancient magic spells that Levenda helped bring out. Levenda says he saw this himself, and he names a man called Larry Barnes in telling it. Michels repeats the story in another episode in a bigger form: he says Levenda received several letters from inside the military, mentions Fort Benning, an Army base, and says they praised the book as "spot on", where Levenda describes just a simple note of congratulations.
stratton-and-lacatski-built-osap-togethe: A secret study program inside the Defense Intelligence Agency, the Pentagon's military spy agency, was built by two officials together, Jay Stratton and Jim Lacatski, and not by Lacatski alone. The program is known as OSAP and looked into unexplained aerial reports. This comes from Eric W. Davis, a physicist who worked on Pentagon UFO studies and says he took part. He says "it was Jim and Jay and their support staff," which would give Stratton a bigger role in the program's beginnings than is usually credited.
stratton-forms-the-uap-task-force-2020: Around 2020 a man named Jay Stratton, who Michels thinks may have been in the Navy, set up the UAP Task Force. UAP, short for unidentified anomalous phenomena, is the government's newer word for UFOs, and Michels describes the task force as an effort to "internally review all of the data here." Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, while tracing how the US government came to take UFOs seriously again.
streak-left-on-the-cliff-by-the-craft-19: When a craft crashed on a mesa near the Archuleta ranch in New Mexico in 1948, it left a streak on the cliff that can still be seen today, Michels says. He tells this himself, drawing on a man named Scott Ramsey, whom he counts as a witness to the site. To Michels the mark is lasting physical evidence that something really came down there.
stress-iq-test-during-air-force-recruitm: A former military helicopter pilot named Jake Barber says that in 1994, during screening to join the Air Force near UCLA in California, he took an intelligence test twice: once normally, and once wearing an oxygen mask sealed over his face with no air coming in. Barber tells this from his own experience, as an example of how recruits were tested for thinking under stress.
strieber-helps-fund-the-first-scientific: In 1978, the author Whitley Strieber says, he and his family helped pay for the first scientific studies of the Shroud of Turin, a linen cloth kept in Turin, Italy, that many believe carries the image of Jesus. Strieber tells it himself: they gave "a few thousand dollars" and followed the work, though he only met the scientists, named as Jackson and Jumper, at fundraisers and never became friends with them.
strieber-s-career-destroyed-which-he-tie: The writer Whitley Strieber, who has written about his own encounters with beings he calls visitors, says his career and life were wrecked from the late 1980s on, and he is "convinced" it has "something to do with" a secretive group known as the Collins Elite. He tells it as his own life and points to the third episode of Beyond, a series made by the film studio MGM, as showing "what happened to me and what it did to my life," which, if he is right, would mean someone set out to ruin him for what he said.
