water-damage-suggests-the-egyptian-monum: The Great Sphinx of Egypt shows weathering that some say could only come from heavy rain, which would make it far older than the usual date of about 4,500 years. The idea comes from the writer John Anthony West, who brought the geologist Robert Schoch to the Giza plateau to look. The writer Graham Hancock says Schoch studied the trench around the Sphinx and concluded it shows "precipitation-induced weathering". Hancock quotes him as saying the monument is "more like 12 and 1/2 thousand years old", from a wet stretch around 12,800 to 11,600 years ago. The researcher Jeffrey Drum points to vertical cracks in the back wall of the enclosure as the sign of a much rainier time. The researcher Randall Carlson says he is "convinced that it is water erosion" and also credits an earlier scholar, Schwaller de Lubicz. The researcher Matt LaCroix, who spoke with Schoch, agrees the Sphinx belongs to "a previous age". Jesse Michels repeats the idea, sometimes placing the damage on the Sphinx's nose. If they are right, someone was building great monuments in Egypt thousands of years before the civilisation usually given credit.
water-found-in-the-osiris-shaft-at-about: There is water below the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt, according to a researcher named Filippo Biondi, who uses satellite radar to scan beneath the pyramids. He says his team found water in the Osiris shaft, a deep tomb shaft cut into the rock at Giza, at roughly 33 to 37 metres down. He gives it as his own team's finding and names no other source.
water-fuelled-microwave-electrothermal-t: A small rocket engine that runs on water, heating it with microwaves to make thrust, has flown in space and worked, according to the scientist John Brandenburg, who says he invented it. Brandenburg tells Michels he got the water-based thruster working himself and that it later flew on a space tug, a small craft that moves satellites around, built by a company called Momentus. If true, it would mean plain water can serve as a working spacecraft fuel.
water-through-piezoelectric-spirals-gene: Filippo Biondi, a scientist who used radar to scan beneath the pyramid of Khafre at Giza in Egypt, suggests that water may once have flowed through spiral structures under it made of piezoelectric material, the kind that gives off electricity when squeezed. He floats it as a possibility, linking it to the pyramid researcher Christopher Dunn. If true, the pyramid would have worked as a kind of power plant.
watergate-document-shredding-at-bendix-a: When the Watergate scandal broke in the 1970s, the political break-in affair around President Nixon, the shredders at a company called Bendix ran overtime, according to the writer Peter Levenda, who is billed on the show as a CIA historian. Levenda says he worked for Bendix at the time and that his whole division "went absolutely nuts because of all the stuff we had on paper." The story is also tied to training troops in Saudi Arabia, though his quoted words are about the shredding, which suggests the company had papers it did not want found.
watergate-used-to-remove-nixon-over-disc: Watergate, the scandal that forced President Richard Nixon from office between 1972 and 1974, is said to have been set up on purpose to get rid of him. Steven Greer, a researcher who campaigns for the release of UFO secrets, says it without naming a source, and gives a reason: Nixon was determined to bring out the truth about UFOs, so he had to be removed. Michels says it too, calling Watergate an inside job and a setup to oust Nixon. He points to Mark Felt, the FBI official who secretly fed information to the reporter Bob Woodward, but he does not say anything about UFOs as the motive.
we-are-watching-you-postcard-1995: Around 1995, while he was shooting the pilot of a TV series, the television writer Bryce Zabel got a postcard at his Los Angeles home with the cover of a book called Flying Eyes on the front and the words "WE ARE WATCHING YOU". Zabel tells this as something that happened to him. To him it suggested that someone was keeping an eye on people making UFO stories in Hollywood.
we-re-the-aquarium-1996: In 1996, at the Los Angeles offices of Dark Skies, a TV series about UFOs, visitors told the show's makers they belonged to a group called "the Aquarium," says the TV writer Bryce Zabel, who was there. He says the men, one he calls JC and another "the captain," asked if he had heard of the Aviary, a circle of insiders tied to UFO stories that had already been shown on television, and then said, "Well, we're the aquarium." If true, it would mean a second hidden group was quietly reaching out to Hollywood about UFOs.
weather-bureau-employees-see-four-metall: In 1947, around the time of Kenneth Arnold's famous sighting of flying objects that year, two employees of the US Weather Bureau, the government's weather service, are said to have seen four metallic discs that were flat on the bottom and domed on top. A guest named Marik von Rennenkampff brings this up without naming a source, as support for the idea that Arnold was not the only one seeing such craft.
weather-data-shows-strong-northerly-wind: Weather records from 2004 show an extremely strong wind out of the north at the height of the object in FLIR1, an infrared video a Navy jet filmed off Southern California, which the story ties to a white oval object shaped like a Tic Tac mint. Marik von Rennenkampff raises the point during a debate about the footage, crediting the analysis to someone named Yannick. The wind matters because it would decide whether the object could have been a balloon simply drifting with the air.
weather-observer-injured-in-an-encounter: In the 1960s, a weather observer working on the Indian Springs testing ranges in the Nevada desert is said to have been hurt in an encounter with something unknown, and then let go from the military on medical grounds. Michels mentions it in passing, without naming a source, while introducing his guest Charles Hall, a former Air Force weather observer who says he spent three years among tall white aliens on those ranges. If it were true, it would mean Hall was not the only observer out there who met something strange, and that one of them paid for it with his health.
webster-hubbell-s-book-on-clinton-s-jfk-: In the 1990s, the story goes, President Bill Clinton and his close associate Webster Hubbell tried to find out two things: who killed President John F. Kennedy, and what is really going on with UFOs. The UFO researcher Steven Greer says Hubbell wrote about this in a book whose title Greer does not remember, and that in it "he admits that he and the president were trying to get to the bottom of a couple things," Kennedy's killing and UFOs. The filmmaker and journalist Jeremy Corbell, in a later episode, tells it more darkly. He says Clinton "really tried until they crushed down Webster Hubble after asking." He does not mention the book or Kennedy. If it is true, even a sitting president could not get answers about UFOs, and someone pushed back on the people who asked.
weekend-meeting-with-dick-cheney-on-why-: In 2003, a CIA officer named Rolf Mowatt-Larssen says he sat down with Vice President Dick Cheney at the White House over a weekend to talk about why the Iraq war was being lost. He tells it first-hand, adding that he came to know Cheney "exceptionally well", to show how close he was to the top of government at the time.
weekly-odni-briefings-for-national-secur: National-security reporters go every week to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the office that oversees the US spy agencies, and get briefed on what they will talk about the following week. That is the claim of Matthew Brown, a guest the episode presents as a Pentagon whistleblower, who speaks of it as something he knows first-hand. If true, it would mean some of the news on these subjects is steered by the intelligence world before it reaches the public.
weinbrenner-deathbed-claim-of-et-bodies-: A man named Weinbrenner is said to have claimed on his deathbed that dead beings from another world are kept at a facility in Utah, which is taken to be Dugway Proving Ground, a military testing range there. A researcher who goes by UAPGerb passes this on, crediting the work of the UFO researchers Grant Cameron and Anthony Bragalia rather than any account of his own. If true, it would place alien bodies in US government hands at a known base.
weinstein-attends-ed-witten-s-first-stri: In 1983 the physicist Ed Witten gave his first lecture on string theory, an idea in physics that the smallest pieces of matter are tiny vibrating strings, at the University of Pennsylvania. The researcher Eric Weinstein says he was in the room, and that he got there by complete accident. He tells it as a first-hand memory of the moment a big idea in physics was starting out.
weinstein-on-rogan-renaissance-technolog: The mathematician Eric Weinstein says that if the US has a secret physics programme, perhaps on gravity and UFOs, it is probably Renaissance Technologies, an investment firm on Long Island founded by the mathematician Jim Simons, which he calls a black hole that hires exactly the specialists, such as differential geometers who study curved space, that such work would need. Michels relays more than once that Weinstein speculated this on Joe Rogan's podcast in 2024 and later tied it to the UFO legacy programme, while Weinstein repeats it in his own words on this show. If true, the hidden science behind recovered craft would sit inside a hedge fund.
weinstein-s-government-funded-training-a: The mathematician Eric Weinstein says the US government paid for his training but now shows no interest in his physics. He says the Office of Naval Research, the Navy's science funding office, paid for his graduate studies, the National Science Foundation, a federal science funding agency, paid for his postdoctoral job, and he believes he was put on a Department of Energy grant, which he calls very unusual for a mathematician and says happened because the mathematician Isidor Singer had one. "None of those people have any interest whatsoever in what I'm saying," he says, which he finds "fascinating."
weinstein-tells-jim-simons-about-chern-s: Shortly before the billionaire mathematician Jim Simons died, the researcher Eric Weinstein says he more or less accused Simons of something tied to Chern-Simons theory, a piece of mathematics that bears Simons's name, and the Einstein-Hilbert equations behind Einstein's gravity. Weinstein tells this as his own meeting, which he links to an invitation to the Simons Center at Stony Brook in New York. In his words: "I more or less accused Jim Simons of this shortly before he died."
weinstein-told-the-same-by-multiple-unre: Eric Weinstein, a researcher and commentator who wants the Pentagon to release its UFO secrets, says that several people with no link to each other have all told him the same thing. He says it while pressing a Pentagon scientist on the show, though in what he says here he does not spell out what the shared claim was. His point is that matching accounts from unconnected sources are harder to brush aside.
wen-ho-lee-espionage-case-1980: John S. Herrington, a former US Secretary of Energy, says a spy named Wen Ho Lee was working inside the Energy Department at Livermore and Los Alamos, two of the government's nuclear weapons laboratories, sometime between the 1980s and the late 1990s. Herrington tells it from his time in office and mentions the former Attorney General Ed Meese in connection with it, as an example of how secrets could leak out of the nuclear labs.
wernher-von-braun-s-project-mars-and-a-l: In 1952, Wernher von Braun, the rocket engineer whom Michels calls a former Nazi and the father of the American space program, published a science fiction novel called Project Mars: A Technical Tale. Michels says the book imagines a future mission to settle Mars led by a figure called "Elon." He tells it himself, without naming a source, in an episode about whether the mind can see ahead in time, where the name stands out as a strange glimpse of the future.
westall-landing-and-intimidation-of-mr-g: In 1966 at Westall, in Australia, a UFO is said to have landed, and a man named Mr. Greenwood is said to have been pressured into silence afterwards. James Fox, who looked into the case himself, brings it up in passing, recalling the time he managed to track down Mr. Greenwood. He gives no more detail, but he tells it as part of a pattern of witnesses being leaned on after sightings.
westall-landing-case-two-witnesses-talk-: In 1966, at Westall in Australia, a crowd of schoolchildren and a teacher are said to have watched a disc-shaped craft in the sky, and some say it landed. James Fox, a documentary filmmaker who investigates UFO cases, went to look into what he calls this "landing case." He says the witnesses he met told him "we've been going at it for 50 years." He later puts the crowd at "300 plus witnesses" watching "this disc zip around in the sky," and credits two others, Shane Ryan and James Rigney. A commentator named Marik von Rennenkampff gives his own summary without naming a source. He says 200 or 300 students and a teacher saw "a silver disc sort of banked on its side" that then took off at 1,000 miles an hour, and he says nothing of a landing. A retired Army officer named Karl Nell brings up Westall secondhand, as an "almost similar identical incident" to another sighting at a school. The case is told because so many ordinary witnesses saw the same thing at once.
wewelsburg-castle-seances-of-himmler-s-s: In the 1930s Heinrich Himmler, head of the SS, the Nazi elite guard, is said to have turned Wewelsburg Castle in Germany into a ritual center for his men. The author Peter Levenda, who writes about the Nazis and the occult, says he visited the castle and filmed a TV program there years ago. He says it was in disrepair when Himmler took it over, that it was rebuilt with concentration camp labor, and that Himmler built a round table for "his 12 knights to sit around and have seances." Jesse Michels tells it in another episode, saying Himmler made the castle a ritual center "complete with a black sun chamber beneath it," a room under the castle, along with the round table for his SS knights. Michels does not mention seances or the camp labor. The tellers bring it up to show how deeply occult belief ran at the top of the Nazi state.
weygandt-s-sergeant-responds-to-uapgerb-: An online researcher who goes by UAPGerb says he emailed a sergeant linked to a man named Weygandt from his pseudonymous "uapgerb" email account, and the sergeant wrote back using UAPGerb's real full name. UAPGerb tells this from his own experience, naming a Sergeant Atkins and a Sergeant Allen, and it suggests someone on the other end already knew who he was.
what-happened-to-the-egg-shaped-craft-ba: An egg-shaped craft that was lifted out of a site is said to have been taken to a secure facility, where it was either destroyed, hidden or buried. A former helicopter pilot named Jake Barber, who says he retrieved it with his own helicopter, tells Michels this, adding that whoever holds it has so many such craft now that this one was not interesting to them.
wheeler-s-it-from-bit-paper-cites-observ: The physicist John Wheeler cited a researcher named Don Hoffman in his 1989 paper known as It from Bit. What he cited was observer mechanics, a framework Hoffman built with colleagues named Bruce Bennett and Chaitan Posh. Hoffman tells this himself, as recognition of his work from a major physicist.
when-prophecy-fails-1950s-ohio-ufo-cult: In the 1950s, a small group in the American Midwest led by a woman named Dorothy Martin believed it had received a prophecy from a UFO that the world would end in 1954. Michels brings it up twice, once calling it a cult founded in Ohio and naming the book When Prophecy Fails, and once crediting the book American Cosmic by the scholar Diana Pasulka, where he gives Martin's name, the year 1954 and the wider Midwest. He offers it as an early example of a modern UFO cult, a sign of how UFO belief can turn into religion.
whistleblower-protections-gutted-from-th: Steven Greer, a longtime campaigner for UFO disclosure, says that in December 2023 Congress nearly wrote protections for UFO whistleblowers into law, but they were gutted when the two chambers merged their versions of the National Defense Authorization Act, the yearly law setting US defense policy and spending. Greer tells it as something he followed closely, crediting the Senate Intelligence Committee with the original push, and says Congress still needs to make those protections law so insiders can come forward.
whistleblower-saw-a-tic-tac-offloaded-fr: A Tic Tac, a white oval craft shaped like the mint, is said to have been unloaded from a big ship, around 1991 as he remembers it, according to the UFO activist Steven Greer, who says an unnamed whistleblower of his saw it happen. If true, it would mean such craft are held, and moved around, by people on Earth.
whistleblower-threatened-with-planted-ch: In 2009, a whistleblower who was about to testify in Washington was frightened off when an SUV pulled up outside his house while his wife was at work and his two young boys were at home. The men in it told him to look at his phone and his computer, and he found them filled with planted child pornography. The UFO activist Steven Greer repeats this as what the man told him, as a sign of how far people will go to keep witnesses quiet.
whistling-ufo-seen-near-aztec: A UFO came in from one direction near Aztec, New Mexico, making a sound that was almost like whistling. That is how an unnamed local witness, who says they saw it themselves, describes it on an episode about a reported crash of a craft with alien bodies in that area, where it would add to the story that something unusual has been seen there.
white-horse-hills-5-300-m-from-the-avebu: The white horse hills of Wiltshire in England, hillsides with large horse figures on them, lie 5,300 metres from the Avebury stone circle complex, an ancient ring of standing stones, and a pyramid researcher named Geoffrey Drumm says this is exactly 3.3 miles. Drumm gives the measurement himself, without naming a source, as a sign that these ancient sites were laid out on purpose with precise distances.
white-house-ai-timeline-manipulator-2020: The idea, floated briefly, is of something like a 'White House timeline manipulator', a system in the American government that could steer which future happens. Michels mentions it himself in a 2026 conversation with the filmmaker Jeremy Corbell, tying it to a man named Matthew Brown, without saying more about what the device is or who runs it. If true, it would mean the government was trying to shape events by reaching across time.
white-house-asks-the-congressman-to-prai: In 2026, the day before the president put out a release of information, the White House called a congressman and asked him to say some positive things about it, according to that congressman, Eric Burlison. Burlison tells Michels this happened to him directly, in the words "can you say some positive things about the president's release tomorrow?" He tells it to show how the government tried to shape the public reaction to what it was releasing.
white-house-registers-aliens-gov: According to Michels, the White House recently registered the web address aliens.gov. He raises it himself, without naming a source, while speaking with a former director of the National Security Agency, the US spy agency that intercepts communications. He offers it as a hint that the government may be getting ready to speak publicly about aliens.
white-house-request-for-presidential-ufo: In 2025 a US congressman named Eric Burlison asked for the same full briefing on UFOs that the president receives, along with visits to the sites involved. Burlison tells it himself: "I'd like a full briefing, the same White House level briefing that the president gets on this topic." If granted, it would let members of Congress see what the president is told.
white-sands-near-earth-satellite-search-: In 1953 a very unusual project began at White Sands Missile Range, a military test site in New Mexico: a search for small unknown objects circling close to Earth, led by the meteor scientist Lincoln LaPaz and the astronomer Clyde Tombaugh. Jesse Michels brings this up himself in a 2025 episode with the astronomer Beatriz Villarroel, and he points to the project's own final report, the Near Earth Satellite Project final report, as his source. He raises it because, if true, it would mean scientists were quietly hunting for unexplained objects near Earth years before any country had launched a satellite.
whitley-strieber-chosen-as-a-disclosure-: The horror writer Whitley Strieber believes he was chosen as a "communication node" for disclosure, the public revealing of what is known about UFOs, and that being a horror writer was part of why. Michels relays this from Strieber's own words, tied to Communion, Strieber's 1980s book about his experiences. If true, it would mean whoever is behind the phenomenon picked its messengers on purpose.
whitley-strieber-s-abduction-books-and-f: In the 1980s, the writer Whitley Strieber put out books, which were later made into films, about his own experience of being abducted by aliens. The podcaster and comedian Joe Rogan mentions this in passing as he describes who Strieber is, as an example of someone who went public with an abduction story.
whitley-strieber-s-blue-beings-the-cobal: The author Whitley Strieber, who has written about his own encounters with otherworldly beings, describes a kind of blue being that he calls the cobalts. Jeffrey Mishlove, a researcher with a doctorate who studies psychic phenomena, mentions this in passing, repeating Strieber's account, as one more type of being that people say they have met.
whitley-strieber-s-ear-implant-evaded-th: Whitley Strieber, who says he has met aliens, says that in San Antonio, Texas, in 1994 or 1996, a doctor named Roger Leir tried to remove an object from his ear, a white disc, and when the doctor touched it with a probe it sank down into his earlobe, all while Anne Strieber filmed it. Strieber tells it firsthand, and Michels, who says the implant shows up on an x-ray and that he has watched the video of the thing "moving at its own," retells it as an implant that dodged the surgeon. If true, it would mean the object was able to move by itself.
whitley-strieber-s-traumatic-abduction-w: The writer Whitley Strieber is said to have described being taken by beings in the 1980s and anally raped, and to still put ointment on the wounds decades later, yet to call the whole experience "a communion." The parapsychologist Jeffrey Mishlove tells this as an example, repeating Strieber's own account. He raises it to show how such encounters can be both traumatic and deeply meaningful to the people who live them.
whitley-strieber-s-uncle-worked-with-gen: The writer Whitley Strieber says his uncle worked very closely with a general named Exon at Wright Field, a military airfield in Ohio, around the 1940s. Michels mentions this in passing and ties it to Strieber's book Communion. The connection matters to Michels because it would put Strieber's own family near the people at the base.
whitley-strieber-tries-to-steal-the-craf: A man named Whitley Strieber once said that when he was near a craft, he wanted to steal it, and somebody behind him started laughing. Grant Cameron, a guest on the show, repeats it as something Strieber told him. It is told as a small, odd detail from Strieber's own experience.
who-ran-the-cia-weird-desk-1960: The CIA, the US foreign intelligence agency, kept an informal "weird desk" for strange topics such as UFOs. From the 1960s on, it was run first by a man named Arthur Lundahl, then by Kit Green, then by Ron Pandolfi. The researcher Grant Cameron gives this line of names without saying where it comes from. If true, the agency had an unbroken chain of people keeping watch on the subject.
whole-earth-catalog-page-187-15th-centur: In the Soap Plant bookstore on Melrose in Los Angeles, the screenwriter Brent Friedman says he found an out-of-print book of 15th-century Scandinavian ghost stories, among them a tale called "Witch Rider." Friedman tells it first-hand and ties the find to page 187 of the Whole Earth Catalog, a well-known catalogue of books and tools. He tells it as one of the strange finds behind his work in Hollywood.
why-borland-came-forward-lives-in-danger: He came forward in 2023 because whistleblowers linked to the Pentagon's group for studying unidentified objects said people's lives were in danger, and because a colleague who had been let into a secret programme lost their job, says Dylan Borland, who tells it as his own reason for speaking out. He mentions Matthew Sullivan and the whistleblower David Grusch, who testified to Congress about hidden UFO programmes, as part of that story.
why-dopsr-let-grusch-talk-about-downed-c: In 2023, David Grusch, a former intelligence officer turned whistleblower, was allowed to say publicly that the US has several downed craft and has recovered dead pilots. The Pentagon office that reviews what former officials may say in public had cleared those statements. Jake Barber, who says he flew a helicopter to recover a UFO, offers an explanation of why that office let Grusch say this, and admits the situation is confusing.
why-site-november-5-was-targeted-1977: In 1977, at a nuclear missile launch site called November 5 in the missile field of Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota, something chose that site on purpose, according to Mario Woods, an Air Force veteran who says he was there and was abducted. He asks why November 5 in particular, and answers that it was the closest to a town, the closest to the launch control center, and the quickest to reach from the other nine missiles, which to him suggests whoever came knew the layout of the base.
wife-s-matching-dream-of-number-cubes-at: In 1978, in the German town of Schwandorf, the wife of the former CIA officer Rolf Mowatt-Larssen is said to have had a dream that matched his own dream of cubes with numbers on them at a church. Mowatt-Larssen repeats what she told him: as she got near the end of the dream, in dim light, with only a few lights on the side of the church, "I saw your desk." He tells it as a sign that the two of them shared the same vision, part of his larger story of seeing across time.
wife-s-wedding-ring-moved-and-found-by-p: In 2024, at their home, the wedding ring of a woman named Kristen Fugal is said to have been moved from where she left it, and then found through prayer. Her husband Brandon Fugal, the owner of a Utah ranch known for strange reports, tells it, relaying what Kristen experienced. He tells it as one of the odd happenings that he says reach beyond the ranch.
wikileaks-email-hillary-clinton-asks-abo: The claim is that an email made public by WikiLeaks, a website that publishes leaked documents, shows the American politician Hillary Clinton asking about the tomb and body of Gilgamesh, a king from ancient Iraqi legend, along with talk of resurrection. The researcher and filmmaker Tim Alberino brings it up without naming a source, and he calls it an email that "allegedly" exists, linked to 2016. He raises it to suggest that powerful people care about ancient remains in Iraq.
wilbert-smith-document-naming-von-neuman: A document connected to Wilbert B. Smith, a Canadian figure, alleges that the mathematician John von Neumann, the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer and the science administrator Vannevar Bush sat on the team trying to reverse-engineer the craft from Roswell, the reported 1947 crash in New Mexico. An unnamed researcher on the show describes the document second hand, saying "he found that document," and hedges on the names with "I think it was." If true, it would put some of the best-known scientists of the era to work on a recovered craft.
wilbert-smith-s-1950-canadian-memo: The story is about a top secret Canadian government memo from 1950, written by a man named Wilbert B. Smith, saying that the US government took flying saucers very seriously. The UFO researcher Steven Greer says the memo "accidentally got declassified" and that he included it in a briefing document of his own. A researcher named Grant Cameron gives what it says. Smith reported that flying saucers exist and are "the most highly classified subject in the United States," rated "two points higher than the H-bomb." Cameron links the memo to people named Robert Sarbacher, Vannevar Bush and Omond Solandt. Both men describe the memo from their research rather than from having been involved. They tell it because, if the memo is what they say, it would be an official paper showing that in 1950 the US ranked UFOs above its most secret weapon.
wilbert-smith-s-secret-role-running-radi: In the 1950s, a Canadian official named Wilbert B. Smith is said to have held a top secret clearance and run radio monitoring in Ottawa, Canada's capital. Grant Cameron, a guest on the show, passes this on from a man named Art Bridge, who told him that Smith "had a super top security clearance" and "ran radio Ottawa." The point of telling it is that Smith would have been a well-placed government insider, not an outsider.
wild-bill-donovan-and-the-original-crash: William "Wild Bill" Donovan, a top figure in the OSS (America's wartime spy service) and one of the founders of the CIA, is said to have helped recover a crashed unknown craft near Magenta in Italy. He is also said to have written the first rules for how such crash recoveries should be handled. Michels tells this from the work of a journalist named Chris Sharp, who says Donovan was "likely" involved, and Michels adds that Donovan was also a Knight of Malta, a member of an old Catholic order of knights. If true, it would mean the plan for gathering up crashed craft existed before the famous cases of the late 1940s.
wild-bill-donovan-parachutes-in-with-a-b: Bill Donovan, the head of America's wartime spy agency, is said to have parachuted into Vietnam with a very rare butterfly collection taped to his chest, a gift for the Vietnamese revolutionary leader Ho Chi Minh. Joe McMoneagle, who worked as a psychic spy for the US Army, tells it second-hand and calls Donovan "John Donovan." He tells it as an example of how strange and personal intelligence work could get.
wilder-penfield-and-false-memories: A doctor named Wilder Penfield, who Michels says was involved in early mind control research, is said to have shown in mice that false memories can be planted. Michels brings this up himself, without naming a source, during a conversation about whether people's memories, such as memories of strange encounters, can be manipulated.
willcutts-review-of-forrestal-s-death-19: After a former US Defense Secretary named Forrestal died at Bethesda Naval Hospital in Maryland in 1949, the Navy held a follow-up inquiry into his death, known as the Willcutts review, written that year. The researcher Richard Dolan says he has read most of its transcript, and he brings it up on Michels' show while arguing that the Defense Secretary's death was tied to UFOs.
william-barr-interviews-epstein-s-cellma: After the financier Jeffrey Epstein died in his New York jail cell in 2019, William Barr, then attorney general (the top law officer) under President Trump, is said to have gone to the cell in person to interview Epstein's last known cellmate, a man named Efrain Reyes. According to Michels, Reyes expressed doubt that Epstein's death was a suicide. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, while pointing out that Barr is the son of a man named Donald Barr, and he raises it as a reason to question the official account of the death.
william-dudley-pelley-s-star-guests-and-: A man named William Dudley Pelley is said to have written a book called Star Guests while he was in prison, sometime in the 1940s, and that book is said to have founded a religion called Soulcraft. The philosopher Jason Jorjani tells this on the show without naming his source, in a conversation about the idea that contact with beings from elsewhere has shaped human religion.
william-gunston-s-tower-of-london-remark: The writer William Gunston, in a history of aircraft engine technology printed in the aviation magazine Air International, is said to have touched on the idea of electrically charging the edges of aircraft wings and then stopped short, saying he would go no further "because I don't want to end up in the Tower of London," the old London fortress once used as a royal prison. Michels brings up the remark himself, crediting that magazine piece. He raises it because, if meant seriously, it would hint that the subject was a guarded state secret in Britain.
william-morris-davis-s-paper-the-value-o: In the 1920s the geologist William Morris Davis wrote a well-known paper called The Value of Outrageous Geological Hypotheses, which argues that wild-seeming ideas are worth taking seriously in science. The researcher Randall Carlson brings it up from memory, calls it "the value of outrageous hypothesis", and says Michels could easily find it as a free download online. He uses it to defend bold theories about Earth's past.
william-steinman-pushed-out-of-aerospace: Michels says that William Steinman, a UFO researcher of the 1980s, lost his place in the aerospace industry because of his UFO research and could never get a job in that field again. Michels tells it himself, without naming a source, in two episodes, in 2025 and 2026. In the second he tells it a little differently, saying Steinman worked at Skunk Works, the secret aircraft design shop of the company Lockheed, was looking into UFOs there, and was fired. Michels tells it as a sign that asking about UFOs could cost a person his career.
william-steinman-s-call-with-eric-walker: Eric A. Walker, a scientist who was president of Penn State University, is said to have admitted on a phone call with the UFO researcher William Steinman that he knew about Majestic 12, a secret panel said to have handled crashed saucers. Michels links the story to Robert Sarbacher, a scientist whose account described someone like Walker, and the call is also remembered for talk of psi, meaning psychic abilities. Michels says that when Steinman asked Walker directly, Walker said he had known about the group for decades. The UFO researcher Grant Cameron dates the call to 1987 and gives Walker's words: "I was there. So what?" and then, "I've known of them for 40 years. Leave it alone." Cameron says this is what convinced him the story is real, since it would mean a senior insider confirmed the group existed.
william-steinman-s-foia-requests-reveal-: An Army group called the Interplanetary Phenomenon Unit is said to have existed and to have handled UFO matters. Its existence, the story goes, came to light in 1986 and 1987 through requests made under the Freedom of Information Act, a US law that lets anyone ask for government records. A researcher named William Steinman is said to have made those requests. The researcher known as UAPGerb tells it this way, naming Steinman and the researcher Kevin Randall among those who uncovered it. Michels repeats it in a later episode, saying "we know due to Bill Steinman and his work" that the unit existed. He places the unit itself in 1947 to 1950 and links the find to Steinman's 1986 book UFO Crash at Aztec. If the records are as described, the Army had an official unit for things from beyond Earth.
william-stephenson-s-caribbean-activitie: In the 1940s a man named William Stephenson was, according to Michels, "doing a lot of stuff in and around the Caribbean, the Bahamas, the Virgin Islands." Michels tells this himself in an episode about Jeffrey Epstein, linking Stephenson to the wartime spy chief Bill Donovan, to scientists such as the engineer Charles Steinmetz and the inventor Thomas Townsend Brown, and to the businessman Robert Maxwell. He brings it up to suggest an old web connecting spies, scientists and the islands that runs forward to later figures.
william-stephenson-telegram-about-townse: During the Second World War an American scientist named Thomas Townsend Brown is said to have parachuted behind enemy lines into Nazi Germany to bring back technology, and a telegram told his wife he had made it. The telegram is said to come from a man named William Stephenson and to be addressed to Brown's wife, Josephine Brown. Michels tells it several times. Once he credits a person named Jan Lundquist as his source. Another time he quotes the telegram as saying "your husband is okay" and calls the trip "a tech retrieval mission". Paul Schatzkin, a writer who has researched Brown's life, tells it through Brown's daughter, Linda Brown. He says the telegram was sent to her mother from the Rockefeller Plaza building in New York and "signed Intrepid, which was William Stephenson's name, code name." Those who tell it see it as a sign that Brown did secret wartime work far beyond his public career.
wilson-denied-need-to-know-though-the-pr: In 1997, Thomas R. Wilson, head of the Defense Intelligence Agency, the Pentagon's military intelligence service, was refused details of a secret program on the grounds that he had no "need to know", the security rule that secrets go only to people whose work requires them, even though the program's money came out of his own director's budget. Eric W. Davis, a scientist who has worked on Pentagon projects and says he was part of these events, tells Michels this, allowing that the refusal on paper was "possible". If true, it would mean a program could hide from the very official paying for it.
wilson-green-works-with-puharich-at-the-: In the 1950s, a man named Wilson Green is said to have worked with a researcher named Puharich at the Round Table, a private research lab, where they were "doing everything." An unnamed researcher on the show says this without giving a source, though he credits Puharich's own journals. He tells it to show who was involved in the lab's early experiments, in an episode about a scientist said to have contacted an alien council.
wilson-meeting-at-the-eg-g-parking-lot-w: In 2002 a physicist named Eric W. Davis met a senior military officer named Thomas R. Wilson, and the meeting is said to have taken place in the parking lot of EG&G, a defense contractor. A document called the Wilson memo is presented as notes of that conversation. Jesse Michels adds, in a 2024 episode with the filmmaker James Fox, that he is "pretty sure" EG&G is where Bob Lazar worked, a man who says he worked on alien craft, which would tie the meeting to one of the best-known claims in the field.
wilson-memo-on-a-private-aerospace-rever: The Wilson memo is a leaked set of notes that describes a secret meeting between Admiral Thomas Wilson, then head of intelligence for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and a physicist named Eric Davis. In it Wilson says he was shut out of a private company program studying UFO technology. The record dates it to 1997, though Michels and others place it in 2002. Michels says the two men met in the parking lot of EG&G, a defense contractor in Las Vegas, and that Wilson was furious at having no oversight of these rogue groups. He adds that the memo turned up among the papers of the astronaut Edgar Mitchell. Davis himself, one of the two men in the meeting, says the notes are '100% accurate.' He gives Wilson's words: Wilson met the program manager, security chief, lawyer and chief scientist, who after long arguing told him it was crash retrieval of 'non-human technology, off-world.' Others tell it from outside. The online researcher UAPGerb backs its core claim that Wilson was denied access, though he puts Wilson at the Defense Intelligence Agency, and he mentions a 'watch committee' of gatekeepers. The researcher Grant Cameron traces how the memo passed from Mitchell to a man named James Rigney in Australia and then to him, around 2019, and the filmmaker Jeremy Corbell says he knew about it early through Mitchell. If true, it would mean a private company held alien technology beyond the military's oversight.
wilsondavis-meeting-outside-eg-g-las-veg: A scientist named Eric Davis and a Navy admiral named Thomas Wilson are said to have held a now infamous meeting outside the Las Vegas special projects headquarters of EG&G, a defense contractor, sometime around 1997 to 2002. Michels says Wilson oversaw "basically all American military technology at the time." Michels tells it himself in passing, without naming a source or saying what was discussed, as one step in the story of secret programs said to hold unexplained craft.
winged-orange-glowing-beings-over-skywat: At skywatches, gatherings where people wait out at night to watch the sky, as many as 20 orange glowing beings that seem to have wings have flown about 25 feet over the group's heads, according to Chris Bledsoe, a man the show describes as attracting UFOs and being studied by NASA. Bledsoe says he was there and saw them himself.
wiseman-fails-to-replicate-sheldrake-s-p: The biologist Rupert Sheldrake ran experiments on a dog said to sense when its owner was coming home, and a psychologist named Richard Wiseman tried to run "the exact same experiments" in England, published them, and got no results. That is how the skeptic Michael Shermer tells it, summarising the published work without naming it, during a debate with Michels. He also mentions the statistician Jessica Utts. For Shermer, the failed repeat is a reason to doubt the psychic dog claim.
wishbone-and-spire-structures-on-lunar-f: A researcher named Maaneli Derakhshani says that photos of the far side of the Moon show a wishbone-shaped structure and spires, and that structures in the Paris Sea and other craters there have unusually precise shapes. He describes them from the images, without naming a source. If he is right, they could be the ruins of something built on the Moon long ago.
with-aquino-at-the-afio-meeting-in-las-v: The writer Peter Levenda, billed on the episode as a historian of the CIA, says he was taken to Las Vegas for a meeting of the Association of Former Intelligence Officers, a group of retired spies, where he was with a man named Michael Aquino. He tells it as something he took part in, and also names a man called John B. Alexander. In his telling, someone said to him: "We're going to go to Vegas. Las Vegas is having a meeting of the Association of Former Intelligence Officers."
witkowski-on-the-bell-project-staff-1940: According to Michels, a secret Nazi wartime project of the 1940s known as the Bell had an SS medical chief named Ernst Grawitz on its staff, and Grawitz was its lead scientist. The SS was the Nazi party's own armed and police force. Michels says this was documented by a Polish journalist named Igor Witkowski, and he tells it twice in 2025, in episodes with the writers Richard Dolan and Jason Jorjani. The second time he adds that Grawitz worked directly under the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele. If true, it would put a senior Nazi medical officer at the head of the project.
witness-burns-as-blue-shifted-light-from: The burns some witnesses get near unexplained craft might come from a warp bubble, a proposed pocket of bent space around a craft that could let it move in unusual ways. The idea is that ordinary visible light is shifted up into ultraviolet, so people get "literally a sunburn." David Grusch, a former intelligence officer who went public about government UFO programs, offers this explanation, which would give a physical cause for injuries that witnesses report.
witness-count-for-the-varginha-ship-and-: In 1996 in Varginha, a town in Brazil, a craft and a strange creature were reportedly seen, and the documentary filmmaker James Fox counts about 12 to 15 witnesses to the ship and up to five to the alien body. Fox, who has investigated the case and interviewed people there, gives these numbers to Jesse Michels. He offers the count as a sign of how many people back the story.
witness-ed-34b-and-40b-scrubbed-from-air: A witness code-named Ed described a joint reverse-engineering program, an effort to take apart unknown craft and learn how they work, run between the Nevada Test and Training Range, a military testing area, and Edwards Air Force Base, with 34 billion and then 40 billion dollars wiped from Air Force accounts between 2012 and 2016. The tale comes from a researcher who goes by the online name UAPGerb and says he once covered Ed's account. If true, huge sums were hidden to fund the program.
witness-ed-contacts-greer-over-suppresse: A witness known only as Ed says he reached out to Steven Greer, a campaigner for UFO disclosure, partly because zero-point energy systems, devices said to draw power from empty space, were being built and then kept hidden. The story is passed on by a researcher who goes by UAPGerb, repeating what Ed told him. If true, it would mean a powerful new energy source is being held back from the public.
witness-ed-tests-reverse-engineered-vehi: A witness known only as Ed is said to have been let into secret programmes from 1998 to 2002 while serving at Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada, in the 98th Range Wing, the unit that runs its testing ranges, and to have worked with vehicles built by copying non-human craft, with links to Edwards Air Force Base and Area 51. A researcher who goes by UAPGerb tells this, passing on Ed's account as it came through the UFO activist Steven Greer, who collects such testimony. If true, it would mean the US military was flight-testing such craft around the turn of the century.
witness-hears-a-buzzing-like-machine-bee: A witness who is not named says they heard a sound from the direction of a craft, a buzzing noise like machine bees. The account is played on an episode with the writer Jason Jorjani, who talks about a secret Nazi flying-saucer program, and the witness tells it as something they heard first-hand, with no place or date given.
witness-returns-with-luiza-and-sees-crea: In 1996 in Varginha, Brazil, a witness went back with a woman named Luiza to the spot where a strange creature had been seen and found its footprint pressed into the ground. The witness, who is not named, tells it first-hand: "in that very spot, I saw the creature's track its foot. I will never forget it." It is one of several accounts of a live being said to have been seen and captured in Varginha that year, and the footprint would be physical sign that something was really there.
witness-saw-lazar-at-s-4-getting-on-a-bu: A man has said on camera that he saw Bob Lazar at work at S-4. Lazar says he worked on alien craft in the late 1980s at S-4, a secret site near the Nevada base known as Area 51. The filmmaker and journalist Jeremy Corbell mentions this in passing: he says he got the man to give his testimony publicly on Ancient Aliens, a television series about visitors from other worlds. If true, it would place Lazar at the site where he says he worked.
witnessed-drowning-suicide-and-va-denial: A former Air Force member named Dylan Borland says that after leaving the Air Force, around 2015 in Pittsburgh, he saw a man drown himself, with several other witnesses, and that he has the police report. He tells it first-hand and also points to his enlisted performance review, the Air Force's regular rating of a service member, and to his medical records from the VA, the US Department of Veterans Affairs, which by his account denied his service. He offers the paperwork to show that his story is backed by records.
witnesses-split-up-and-reassigned: John Blitch, a scientist who worked for DARPA, the Pentagon's advanced research agency, says that when military people witness something unexplained they are split up and sent to different posts so they cannot talk to each other. He gives as examples two people he calls Terry and Toby, and two others named Mario Woods and Michael Johnson, without naming a source. If true, it would show the military working to keep witnesses from comparing their stories.
witten-townsend-brown-s-antigravity-bism: In the 1950s, a man named Louis Witten says, Wright Field, a military airfield, hired him to work on gravity, and a man named Thomas Townsend Brown had an unusual form of bismuth, a metal, that seemed to show anti-gravity properties. Michels passes this on from what Witten says, and the story also ties in a company called the Martin Corporation. If true, it would mean the military was quietly chasing anti-gravity research decades ago.
wobbling-craft-may-have-gone-into-autopi: In 1948, near Aztec, New Mexico, a craft said to have crashed there was wobbling as it flew, both before and after it passed over the Archuleta Ranch, and one theory holds that it then switched into a kind of autopilot. A researcher named Scott Ramsey, who has studied the alleged Aztec crash, describes this theory without naming its source. If true, it would explain how the craft is said to have flown due north and come down in a soft landing.
woman-saw-three-plus-signs-rolling-on-ro: In Sweden in the 1930s, a woman is said to have seen three objects shaped like plus signs rolling along a road. The Swedish UFO researcher Clas Svahn tells it second-hand: the account came to him through his mother, whom he says he called to ask about it. If true, it would be a strange sighting from well before UFOs were widely talked about.
woman-tries-to-kidnap-bledsoe-after-a-co: Chris Bledsoe, a man the show describes as attracting UFOs, says that as he walked out the door after speaking at a conference, "this mad lady comes running up to me and tries to kidnap me." He tells it twice as something that happened to him, and in one telling he names the event as what he calls the PSI games, which he says as "sigh games," and places it that year, 2025.
woman-with-black-undulating-eyes-at-foot: A screenwriter named Brent Friedman says he lowered the paper he was reading in bed and saw a woman standing at the foot of the bed, her eyes two black, undulating circles. He tells Michels this happened to him. In another telling of the same night he describes her eyes as like the cosmos, says she pinned him to the bed, places it in a bungalow off Melrose early in his writing career, and calls her the witch rider.
women-believe-their-eggs-were-harvested-: A woman named Juliet Byron says she was taken in September 2002 to Zorro Ranch, a New Mexico ranch the episode ties to the financier Jeffrey Epstein, and that she thinks her eggs were taken there. She links this to the reported cloning of a first baby, called Eve, that December, and says no one ever heard anything about it again. A guest named Jay Anderson relays the same thing, saying she and other women believe their eggs were being harvested for human cloning, which if true would point to secret breeding experiments at the ranch.
woods-s-partner-frozen-at-the-wheel-1977: In 1977 at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota, a man named Michael Johnson froze stiff at the wheel of a vehicle, so locked up that his partner could not pry his hand loose, according to that partner, Mario Woods. Woods says he was there and even tried pulling Johnson's hand off the steering wheel. He tells it as part of a strange encounter at the base that seemed to paralyse a man in place.
woomera-range-chief-s-grandfather-in-sec: A man named Rhys Dalton Morgan, who ran Woomera, a rocket and weapons testing range in Australia, says his grandfather took part in secret UFO investigations for the British government in Britain in the late 1940s and 1950s. The Australian journalist Ross Coulthart passes this on from what Morgan told him. If true, it would mean Britain was quietly studying UFOs soon after the Second World War.
workers-had-severe-reactions-to-touching: People working on a recovered flying craft at S4, a secret site in the Nevada desert, apparently had severe physical reactions just from touching it. Bob Lazar, who says he worked at S4 between 1987 and 1989 studying such craft, tells it to Michels as something he was told rather than something he saw.
working-beside-hunt-s-cia-colleague-arth: Around 1979 the writer Peter Levenda worked in Queens, New York, beside a man named Arthur Hawkberg who, he later learned, had been a colleague of the CIA officer E. Howard Hunt at a Washington firm, the Robert Mullen Corporation, that Levenda calls a front. Levenda tells it from his own experience, saying Hawkberg "turns out to have been E. Howard Hunt's colleague," which would put him a step away from the intelligence world without knowing it.
working-next-to-the-z-machine-at-sandia: He used to work right next to the Z machine at Sandia National Laboratories, a US government research lab in New Mexico, says John Brandenburg, a scientist who argues that Mars once had life that was wiped out by nuclear war. The Z machine is a huge device there that releases enormous bursts of electrical power, and he mentions it in passing as part of his own working background.
world-commerce-corporation-founded-1945: In 1945, wartime spy chiefs set up a company called the World Commerce Corporation, with William Donovan, head of America's wartime intelligence service, and William Stephenson, a British intelligence chief, on its board, and Allen Dulles, later head of the CIA, as its lawyer. The researcher Jason Simosa tells this twice: once he also names a board member called Ambrose, and once he says the company was renamed in 1947, places it in Panama, adds Charles Hambro, and credits the writers Peter Levenda and Peter Dale Scott. If true, it would mean the men behind wartime spying kept working together through a private company after the war.
world-commerce-corporation-maynard-corpo: A network of businesses called the World Commerce Corporation, linked to another called the Maynard Corporation, worked as a secret international group, according to Michels, who calls it "this Caribbean constellation of shell sort of companies." He tells this himself, crediting the book Secret Machines, while talking with a Pentagon whistleblower named Matthew Brown, and ties the network to a man named Otto Scorzani. If true, it would point to a hidden private web behind secret programs.
world-forum-created-by-mikhail-gorbachev: A man named Chris Bledsoe, who says UFOs show up around him, tells Michels about a World Forum that he says the former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev created. According to what Bledsoe was told, it was a five-year event that ran from 1995 to 2000 and ended in New York City "when they dropped the ball", meaning the New Year's ball drop. He brings it up as a gathering of world leaders tied to the other events in his story.
world-tree-myth-of-survivors-climbing-in: Many old myths around the world tell of a world tree: a great catastrophe comes, and humanity survives by climbing the tree up into the heavens. A researcher of ancient catastrophes named Randall Carlson brings up the motif in passing, without naming a source. He offers it as one of the stories that may hold a memory of a real disaster in the deep past.
world-war-ii-foo-fighters-1940: During the Second World War, pilots reported strange lights, later called foo fighters, that seemed to follow their planes. The journalist Nick Cook describes them over Germany as "balls of light that rose up out of the countryside" and "appeared to have some kind of intelligent control." The scientist John Brandenburg says they were "commonly spotted" while radar beams filled the sky, yet none was ever reported to crash, and he uses that to argue against the idea that radar brings these objects down. Michael Shermer, a well-known skeptic, raises them only to say it would be good to have explanations for what the pilots saw.
worldwide-sphere-reports-after-the-2021-: After a 2021 broadcast, people around the world are said to have come forward saying they were seeing spheres in the sky. The journalist Ross Coulthart says he got phone calls, messages and emails from all over the world, including from "a beautiful guy in Africa" who told him they were seeing these spheres. He tells it as a sign that the sightings were not limited to one place.
woven-ceramic-fiber-optic-strip-from-ros: In the 1950s, in a store in London, Wisconsin, a woven strip of fiber optic material about a yard long, said to come from the 1947 Roswell crash in New Mexico, was shown around. Charles Hall, a former Air Force man who says he lived among aliens near Area 51, says he saw it himself as a boy in the summer between fifth and sixth grade. He says it was brought back from Roswell by the man who ran the store, a childhood friend of Ray Palmer, whom Hall believes was the editor of Flying Saucers magazine.
wrecks-carrying-liquor-including-wine-fr: Old shipwrecks on the floor of the Baltic Sea were carrying liquor, including what is said to be one of the oldest wines in the world, from the 1600s. A treasure hunter named Dennis Asberg says he found it himself around 2005, working with a man named Peter Lindberg, as part of his story of what lies on that seafloor.
wright-air-development-center-anti-gravi: Michels says that in the 1950s the Wright Air Development Center, an Air Force research base in Dayton, Ohio, had a dedicated team of physicists working on anti-gravity, citing the physicist Joshua Goldberg. He tells it himself in two episodes, in 2024 and 2025. In the second he adds that the team included the physicist Louis Witten, father of the famous physicist Ed Witten, and ties Witten to the anti-gravity division of the Research Institute for Advanced Study, a research arm of the aircraft maker Martin Company. He raises it to show that the military took anti-gravity seriously at a time when UFO sightings were drawing attention.
wright-field-consultant-lives-with-brown: In the 1950s, a technical consultant named Charles Wyatt Miller, from Wright Field, an American military air base and research center, is said to have lived with a family named Brown all the time. Michels passes this on from Linda Brown, a member of that family, while asking whether the atomic scientist Robert Oppenheimer worked on UFOs. Having a military expert in the house at all times would suggest the family's work was being closely watched by the Air Force.
wright-field-engineers-and-strange-hiero: Between about 1943 and 1947, people at Wright Field, an Army air base in Ohio, were reportedly talking about a material they had never seen before, marked with strange hieroglyph-like symbols. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, during a debate with a skeptic, pointing out that the same base rebuilt the German pulse jet engine, a simple jet engine design, in 1943. He tells it to suggest that engineers who were already experts at copying foreign technology were handling something stranger, even before the famous crash at Roswell in 1947.
wright-field-reverse-engineers-german-pu: In 1943, engineers at Wright Field, a US military aircraft research base, reportedly took apart a German pulse jet and worked out how to build it. A pulse jet is a simple jet engine that runs on rapid bursts of burning fuel. Michels says this himself, without naming a source, in an episode asking whether Oppenheimer worked on UFOs. The researcher UAPGerb tells it in nearly the same words, also without a source. It comes up to show that the base already knew how to copy foreign technology it had never seen before, which matters to stories that later claims about reverse-engineering are built on.
wright-patterson-as-nuclear-antigravity-: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio is said to have become, in the 1950s, a nuclear engineering test site and a research center for antigravity, meaning technology to cancel or control gravity. Michels adds that it was also home to Blue Book, the US Air Force's study of UFO reports in the 1950s and 60s. In a second episode he says the base is where material from the reported 1947 crash at Roswell, New Mexico, was taken, and there he leaves out the nuclear and Blue Book parts. He tells both versions himself, without naming a source, to show that this one base keeps turning up in the UFO story.
wright-patterson-as-reverse-engineering-: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio is said to have been the place where, from the 1940s on, the US military brought captured enemy machines so its engineers could take them apart and work out how to copy them. Michels says this himself, without naming a source, in his interview with David Grusch, a former intelligence officer who has said the government holds craft that were not made by humans. The point is that if the military ever recovered such a craft, this base would be the natural place for it to end up.
writing-the-eulogy-for-one-of-the-invisi: Some time in the 2010s, one of the people who did hidden government work died, a person whose own family never knew what they did, and Diana Pasulka, a researcher who studies religion and UFO belief, says she wrote the eulogy. Pasulka tells it first-hand: while she knew a man she calls Tyler, she met others like him she named "the Invisibles", people whose real jobs stayed secret even from those closest to them. She tells it to show how fully such work can disappear from view.
writing-the-physics-of-angels-with-matth: The biologist Rupert Sheldrake says that he and the theologian Matthew Fox wrote the book The Physics of Angels by picking the most interesting passages about angels from old Christian writers such as Dionysius the Areopagite, Thomas Aquinas and Hildegard of Bingen. Sheldrake, who co-wrote it, says they then "discussed each short passage as a dialogue and that's what the book is really," an attempt to bring old ideas of angels into talk with modern science.
writing-to-bob-lazar-about-his-experienc: Richard Barth, a former nuclear missile guard who says he was abducted by aliens, says he once wrote to Bob Lazar, a man known for saying he worked on alien craft, about his own experience. Barth, who says the name as "Bob Salazar," tells it himself and stresses he wanted nothing from it: "I'm not in this for anything."
written-incident-report-at-colonel-sprak: A nuclear weapons guard named Mario Woods says that in 1977, after a night incident at a missile site, he was called into a Colonel Spraker's office at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota and handed forms. He says he was told to "write down every single thing that happened on that site tonight from the time you got this alarm to the completion," but was never given a copy. Woods tells it as his own experience, also naming a Jack Reed, and it would mean an official written record of the night exists somewhere.
wsj-claim-that-air-force-hazing-rituals-: A 2025 Wall Street Journal article titled "The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology", by the reporter Joel Schectman, claims that hazing rituals inside the US Air Force explain much of America's widespread UFO lore. Michels walks through that claim on the show, calling it the article's "second claim". In a later episode he says, without naming the reporter, that the article actually makes him optimistic, because he finds the hazing explanation "really interesting".
wtc-resident-artist-s-painting-of-planes: The story goes that an artist working inside the World Trade Center made a piece showing planes flying into his own body, not long before planes hit the towers on September 11, 2001, and then died there that morning. Michels tells it in an episode with the scientist Rupert Sheldrake. He says the towers had an arts program, and that the artist showed himself as a Tuskegee Airman, one of the Black American pilots of the Second World War, with old fighter planes all flying into him, 12 days before 9/11. The writer Eric Wargo, who studies dreams and seeing the future and wrote a book called Time Loops, tells it in two episodes with more detail. He names the artist as Michael Richards and calls the work a sculpture, titled Tar Baby vs. St. Sebastian, rather than a painting. Wargo says the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council gave studio space in the towers to groups of 15 artists for six months at a time, and that Richards "alone among those artists" stayed in his studio the night of September 10th and was killed the next morning. They tell it as a possible case of an artist sensing his own future.
wwii-crash-retrieval-of-enemy-technology: The skeptic Michael Shermer recalls that during World War II the United States captured Japanese Zero fighter planes in the Aleutian Islands off Alaska shortly before the Battle of Midway, as an example of how governments recover and study enemy technology. He tells it from general history, without naming a source. He brings it up to show where the idea of secret crash retrievals has an ordinary, wartime model.
x-files-pilot-craft-design-based-on-john: A secret aircraft design called the XF-131 appeared in the very first episode of the television series The X-Files in 1993, and the design was allegedly based on true stories from a man named John Duza, also spelled Desouza. An online UFO researcher who goes by UAPGerb tells this without naming a source. He says that a designer named Bill McDonald was hired to put the craft in the episode, and he credits the show's creator, Chris Carter, which would mean a real secret craft found its way into a TV show.
xerxes-and-alexander-visited-the-sites: Ancient sites around Lake Van in eastern Turkey were visited by Xerxes, the Persian king, and Alexander the Great, along with many other famous figures through history. The researcher Matt LaCroix mentions this in passing without naming a source. He tells it to show that great rulers knew these places and thought them important long ago.
y-12-complex-at-oak-ridge-and-kirkpatric: A researcher who goes by UAPGerb lists the Y-12 complex, a government nuclear site at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, as the last of the places he believes are tied to the Pentagon's secret UFO work. He links it to Sean Kirkpatrick, the first head of the Pentagon's UFO investigation office, who moved there after leaving that job around 2023 to 2025, and he gives this without naming a source, as a hint that the site matters to the subject.
y-12-oak-ridge-legacy-program-studying-t: A man says he worked under the Y-12 complex at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, a US government nuclear site, on a long-running secret UFO program that studies the outer skin of two recovered saucer-shaped craft of non-human origin. A researcher who goes by UAPGerb passes this on to Michels from what the man has stated, and links it to the private research contractors MITRE and Battelle, which do government work. If true, it would mean the US holds and studies non-human craft.
yahweh-acknowledges-the-gods-of-egypt-in: In the Bible's Book of Exodus, in chapter 12 as he remembers it, the Hebrew God, Yahweh, tells Moses that he will bring his wrath down on the gods of Egypt. The researcher Luke Caverns reads this to mean that Yahweh recognises the Egyptian gods as real. If so, the old scripture would be treating other gods as beings that actually existed.
yanomami-wusinari-insect-beings-and-mult: The Yanomami, a people of the Amazon rainforest, describe beings they call the wusinari, insect-like beings, among crowds of dancing spirits. The neuroscientist Andrew Gallimore brings this up, without naming a source, while talking about the psychedelic drug DMT. He mentions it because such beings resemble the ones people report meeting on DMT.
yelin-group-meditation-synchronized-bina: About 30 people meditated together outdoors at a place called Yelin, all listening to the same binaural sound (two slightly different tones, one in each ear) at once, and are said to have made contact with glowing orbs. Jordan Jose, who says he was taken into a UFO program as a child, tells this as a session he led. In his words: "I took a group of about 30 people."
yellow-orb-tags-along-with-atlas-launch-: In 1964 at Vandenberg Air Force Base in California, as the second stage of an Atlas rocket fired, a yellow orb came over and followed the missile. Richard Barth, a former guard of nuclear missiles, says he saw it himself, and tells it as a sign that something was watching American missile tests.
yeltsin-asks-about-his-trip-up-there-199: Around 1997 or 1998, inside the Kremlin, the seat of Russia's government in Moscow, Russia's president Boris Yeltsin told a regional leader, "It's been reported to me that you've been up there." The man telling it is Kiran Ilum Xenov, once president of one of Russia's republics, who says he was taken by aliens in 1997 and that Yeltsin asked him about it to his face. If true, it would mean word of the abduction reached the top of the Russian state.
young-hitler-and-lanz-von-liebenfels-s-o: In Vienna in the early 1900s, a young Adolf Hitler is said to have visited Lanz von Liebenfels, the founder of an occult group called the Order of the New Templars, in his office. The researcher and author Peter Levenda tells it from his own book Unholy Alliance, saying a source "said that he actually visited" Lanz in his office, without naming that source. If true, it would tie the young Hitler directly to occult circles.
young-people-gathered-to-pilot-craft-at-: Very young people are said to be picked out from around the world and brought to secret, unacknowledged military sites, so-called black facilities, where they can fly unusual craft better than adults can. The philosopher Jason Jorjani repeats this as one of the "wild stories" he has heard, without naming who told him. If true, it would mean a hidden program to train children to pilot these craft.
younger-dryas-comet-impact-12-800-years-: The idea is that about 12,800 years ago, near the end of the last ice age, Earth passed through the trail of debris from a comet that was breaking apart, and the impacts changed the world. This is known as the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, named after a sudden cold period of that time. The writer and researcher Graham Hancock lays it out, crediting the Comet Research Group, a team of scientists who study the idea. Michels tells it a little differently: he says it may have been a comet blowing up in the air, coming from the Taurid meteor stream (a stream of space debris Earth crosses each year), and that it may have wiped out an early civilization, crediting Hancock, the researcher Randall Carlson and the ancient Greek philosopher Plato.
younger-dryas-impact-caused-the-great-fl: The claim is that something from space hit the earth around 12,000 years ago, at the start of a sudden cold spell called the Younger Dryas, and that this impact caused the great flood remembered in old myths and wiped out an earlier human civilization. The broadcaster Joe Rogan says it on the show in his own words. Talking about a threat too big for anyone to stop, he says, "that's probably what happened during the younger dryas impact," and he connects it to ancient flood stories, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Michels' co-host, a defense and aerospace engineer who goes by the pseudonym Jack, mentions the same idea more briefly as "the reset 12,000 years ago". He credits it to the researcher Randall Carlson and the writer Graham Hancock and does not say what caused it. The flood tale in the Epic of Gilgamesh, in E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation, is told by the flood survivor Utnapishtim: the great gods decide "to make a wind-storm," a rain-flood falls, "a black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up" with the storm god Adad thundering inside it, and the Anunnaki, whom the translator calls star-gods, "brandished their torches" and "with their glare they lighted up the land." The epic does not describe anything striking the earth. If the idea were true, human history would be much older than we think, and a catastrophe would have erased it.
zahari-greets-john-paul-at-their-first-m: When a nonspeaking young person named Zahari walked into a house in Georgia in 2023 and met another named John Paul for the first time, he greeted him like an old friend, and the two said their friendship had been built on "the hill," a place the children describe meeting in their minds. The filmmaker Ky Dickens, who made The Telepathy Tapes, a documentary about nonspeaking children said to read minds, tells it to Michels as it was told to her. If true, it would suggest the children had been in touch by telepathy before ever meeting.
zahi-hawass-pumps-out-the-osiris-shaft-a: Under Giza in Egypt there is a deep shaft with several levels, called the Osiris shaft. A team led by a man named Zahi Hawass pumped all the water out of it so they could lift the lid off a stone container on the third level, according to the researcher Jeffrey Drum. Drum tells it as part of his case that something important lies beneath the pyramids.
zalce-jailed-five-days-by-the-mexican-na: A man named Jose Zalce, who speaks on an episode about small three-fingered bodies found in Peru, says the Mexican Navy jailed him for about five days in the 2020s. He tells it himself, saying they called him a liar who was "putting in risk the honorability of the whole system of the Navy," which would mean he was punished for speaking out.
zalce-maria-s-dna-is-30-completely-diffe: DNA tests on one of the large three-fingered mummified bodies from Peru, known as Maria, are said to show that around 17 percent matched known DNA while 30 percent was completely different. A researcher named Jose Zalce, who says he worked on the bodies, tells Michels this, which if true would point to something not wholly human. In a second telling he puts the known share at about 70 percent, citing someone he names as David Ron Hell, and lists matches to chimpanzee, bonobo, another African chimpanzee and a South Asian primate.
zamparini-s-wheat-field-where-a-spaceshi: An Italian man named Maurizio Zamparini had a wheat field where a spaceship landed several times in the late 1990s, and he showed the field to Kiran Ilum Xenov, a former president of a republic inside Russia. Xenov repeats what Zamparini told him and showed him, and says there were golden plates with imprints of the landings and photographs taken by scientists, which would be physical traces of the visits if true.
zanesville-metal-seen-moving-under-a-mic: A piece of metal from Zanesville, Ohio, was seen moving on its own under a microscope, according to Chris Bledsoe, a man who says he draws UFOs to him. Bledsoe tells Michels he watched it in real time, saw different types of material, and that one piece was moving. He tells it as a sign the metal is something stranger than ordinary matter, though he does not say when it happened.
zero-gravity-bonding-of-ceramic-to-metal: Scientists are said to have worked out how to bond ceramic to metal in zero gravity, in space with NASA, the US space agency, and then to put human DNA into the ceramic for use in medical implants. Chris Bledsoe, a man who says UFOs appear around him, repeats this from what someone told him: "they figured out in zero gravity how to bond ceramic to metal." He tells it as an example of advanced technology said to have come out of secret work.
zero-point-drives-work-as-time-machines: The idea is that a zero-point drive, an imagined engine that would draw power from the energy said to fill empty space, would also work as a time machine. If so, craft seen as UFOs might be visitors from another time. The philosopher and researcher Jason Jorjani raises it in passing, crediting a book on UFOs and time travel by an author named Michael Masters, which Jorjani says he cites in his own book, Closer Encounters.
zigzagging-light-during-fourth-of-july-f: During Fourth of July fireworks in 2000, at a park along a dry creek bed near his home, a light started moving in a zigzag, according to Richard Barth, a former nuclear missile guard who says he was abducted by aliens. Barth says he saw it himself, mentions a man named Roger in the telling, and describes how "it starts into a zigzag," a movement fireworks would not make.
zimbardo-s-stanford-prison-experiment-19: Michels brings up the Stanford Prison Experiment of 1971, in which the psychologist Philip Zimbardo had students play prison guards and prisoners, as 'all very similar' to other projects he was discussing. He mentions it himself, in passing and without a source, in a 2026 episode about UFO secrecy and a secret society. He places it alongside those projects as part of a pattern of experiments on how people behave.
ziusudra-utnapishtim-s-ark-lands-in-the-: A researcher named Matt LaCroix says on the show that the ark of the Mesopotamian flood hero, called Ziusudra in one version and Utnapishtim in another, came to rest "in the Mount Ararat region" of Armenia and Turkey, the same area where the Bible puts Noah's ark. In E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation of the Epic of Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim is the "man of Shurippak," and his ship sails "to the land of Nisir," where "the mountain of Nisir held the ship." The epic never names Ararat, which comes from the Bible's "mountains of Ararat," and never uses the name Ziusudra.
zodiac-crash-retrieval-program-1998: In 1998, UFO Magazine published a story about a man called Sedge Masters who was brought into a secret program named Zodiac that recovered crashed UFOs, a story linked to the American defense company TRW. The writer used a fake name, Greg Halifax. A researcher who goes by UAPGerb describes the article and mentions the UFO historian Richard Dolan, since the story would point to a private-company program for recovering crashed craft.
zorro-ranch-breeding-program-claims-2000: Women say they were taken to Zorro Ranch, the New Mexico property of the financier Jeffrey Epstein, as part of a breeding program in which Epstein meant to make them pregnant with children of superior genetics. A philosopher named Jason Jorjani tells Michels this is what the women claim, and if true it would mean Epstein was running a eugenics project. In his own article "Ocean Outlaw: A Portrait of Ghislaine Maxwell", published 29 July 2025, Jorjani states it in his own voice, "Epstein planned to impregnate multiple women at his New Mexico 'Zorro Ranch'", says it was modeled on the Lebensborn project of the Nazi SS and inspired by the transhumanist ideas of people like George Church, and names no such women and cites no source.
zulu-legend-that-the-moon-brought-us-out: The Zulu people of southern Africa are said to have a legend that the moon brought humanity out of the Younger Dryas, a sudden return to ice-age cold near the end of the last ice age, and steadied Earth's climate. Michels tells this himself, without naming a source, in an episode with the writer Randall Carlson about the idea that the moon is an alien spaceship. If true, it would mean an old legend remembers the moon acting on purpose to save life on Earth.
